issue.title: $ --help / $ -h fail with 'Unknown wrapper option' (usage only shown with no arguments)
issue.body:
## Problem

`$ --help` and `$ -h` are rejected, both on 0.35.4 and on the latest release, 0.36.0:

```
$ npx -y start-command@0.36.0 --help
Error: Unknown wrapper option: --help
$ $ -h
Error: Unknown wrapper option: -h
```

The usage text is printed only when `$` runs with **no** arguments. `--help` is the first thing people (and agents) try, and `js/src/lib/substitutions.lino` itself references `$ --help` (around lines 301 and 307), so the docs promise something the parser rejects.

In our case an automation wanted to check the available flags (`--detached`, `--image`, …) during an incident and got an error instead of help.

## Expected

- `$ --help` / `$ -h` print the same usage as `$` with no arguments, and exit 0.
- Only as wrapper options before `--`. `$ -- grep --help` must still run `grep --help`.
- Same in the Rust implementation (`rust/src/lib/args_parser.rs`).
- A test for both flags.

We need to download all logs and data related about the issue to this repository, make sure we compile that data to `./docs/case-studies/issue-{id}` folder, and use it to do deep case study analysis (also make sure to search online for additional facts and data), in which we will reconstruct timeline/sequence of events, list of each and all requirements from the issue, find root causes of the each problem, and propose possible solutions and solution plans for each requirement (we should also check known existing components/libraries, that solve similar problem or can help in solutions).

If there is not enough data to find actual root cause, add debug output and verbose mode if not present, that will allow us to find root cause on next iteration.

Each issue must contain reproducible examples, workarounds and suggestions for fix the issue in code. Also double check to fully apply requirements to entire codebase, so if we have issue in multiple places, it should be fixed in all them.

issue.title: $ --upload-log uploads execution logs without secret sanitization
issue.body:
## Problem

`$ --upload-log <execution>` uploads the stored execution log **as is**. `js/src/lib/log-uploader.js` runs `gh-upload-log <logPath>` with no secret sanitization. These logs hold whatever the command printed: environment dumps, tokens echoed by tools, `git remote -v` with credentials, API keys in error messages. For hive-mind tasks, that means agent transcripts.

hive-mind sanitizes before every upload: `uploadLogWithGhUploadLog()` streams the log through its credential sanitizer, and a fail-closed scan (`sanitizeForPublication`, secretlint plus known-token checks) runs before anything is published. `$ --upload-log` skips all of that, so a user who uploads a task log with `$` instead of the bot can leak secrets. That is easy to do when the bot is down, which is exactly when people use `$ --list` / `$ --status` / `$ --upload-log`. Even private gists can be shared by URL.

Found while building automatic dead-task reports in link-assistant/hive-control-center `auto-fix`. It uses hive-mind's sanitizing uploader instead of `$ --upload-log` for this reason.

## Reproduce

```sh
$ -- sh -c 'echo GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzAB'
$ --upload-log <uuid>   # open the uploaded gist: the fake token is there verbatim
```

## Fix

- Sanitize into a private temp file (0600) before uploading. Use a streaming, block-wise sanitizer, since logs reach 100+ MB. Cover known token formats (GitHub `gh[pousr]_…`, `github_pat_…`, OpenAI/Anthropic keys, AWS keys, JWTs, `Authorization:` headers) plus the values of known secret environment variables. Upload the sanitized copy, never the original.
- Fail closed: if the sanitizer errors, do not upload.
- Default to private uploads and say so in `--help`. Offer `--no-sanitize` only as an explicit opt-out.
- Consider reusing hive-mind's sanitizer (`src/token-sanitization.lib.mjs`, `src/log-sanitize-worker.lib.mjs`) or moving it into a shared package.

We need to download all logs and data related about the issue to this repository, make sure we compile that data to `./docs/case-studies/issue-{id}` folder, and use it to do deep case study analysis (also make sure to search online for additional facts and data), in which we will reconstruct timeline/sequence of events, list of each and all requirements from the issue, find root causes of the each problem, and propose possible solutions and solution plans for each requirement (we should also check known existing components/libraries, that solve similar problem or can help in solutions).

issue.title: Support --label KEY=VALUE for docker isolation (and default start-command.* labels) so callers can attribute task containers, also after $ --resume
issue.body:
## Problem

`$ --isolation docker` gives callers no way to put **labels** on the task container. `--env` exists, `--label` does not (start-command 0.36.0, `src/lib/args-parser.js`, `src/lib/docker-runtime-args.js`). The container's identity is only its name (the `--session` value, or `<name>-resume-<n>` after `$ --resume`).

A supervisor that launches many tasks through `$` (here the hive-mind Telegram bot) therefore cannot attribute running containers with `docker ps --filter label=…`. It matters exactly when the execution store is unreliable, as in #193: a resumed container keeps running while `$ --status` / `$ --list` report the previous attempt (`executed 137`). In link-assistant/hive-mind#2917, four running `/codex` task containers were counted as **0** by the bot's queue and `/limits`. The bot's in-memory registry had already reported them finished, and `pgrep` cannot see a sibling container's processes. The bot then kept dispatching new tasks onto a host that had just OOM-killed dockerd.

## Reproduction

```sh
$ --version                                   # 0.36.0
$ --isolation docker --image alpine:3.20 --session demo-1 --detached \
    --label hive-mind.tool=codex -- sleep 600
# → Unknown wrapper option: --label (the task never starts)

# Without the label it starts, but nothing on the container says what it is:
$ --isolation docker --image alpine:3.20 --session demo-1 --detached -- sleep 600
docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.Labels}}' demo-1
# → only the image's labels; no session, uuid or caller-provided attribution
```

## Workaround (used by hive-mind#2917)

Pass the attribution as environment variables with the existing `--env`, then read them back with `docker inspect`:

```sh
$ --isolation docker --session "$UUID" --detached \
    -e HIVE_MIND_TOOL=codex -e HIVE_MIND_TASK_URL=https://github.com/o/r/issues/1 -- solve …
docker ps -q --no-trunc | xargs docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{json .Config.Env}}'
```

This works across `$ --resume`. `docker commit` copies the container's `Config.Env` (and `Config.Labels`) into the snapshot image config, so `<name>-resume-<n>` inherits them; this was checked with docker 29.8.0. It is still a workaround. Env cannot be filtered server-side (`docker ps --filter env=` does not exist), so every running container must be inspected. The values are also visible to the task's own processes.

## Suggested fix

1. Add a repeatable `--label <KEY=VALUE>` (docker only), parsed like `--env`. Push `['--label', value]` in `buildDockerRuntimeArgs()`, so both `docker run` and the snapshot resume path in `execution-resume.js` (which already calls `buildDockerRuntimeArgs({ ...opts, resourceLimits })`) apply it. Store the labels in the execution record next to `env`, so `$ --resume` re-applies them even if the image config is replaced.
2. Always add start-command's own labels, for example:
   - `start-command.session=<session name>`
   - `start-command.root-session=<name without -resume-<n> suffixes>`
   - `start-command.uuid=<execution uuid>`
   - `start-command.resume-count=<n>`

   `docker ps --filter label=start-command.root-session=<uuid>` would then find the live container of a session chain, even when the execution record is stale (#193).
3. Optionally, let `$ --status <name>` fall back to `docker inspect` liveness for a docker execution whose record is terminal while a `<name>-resume-*` container is running.

Related: #193 (resume starts the container but fails to save the record), link-assistant/hive-mind#2917.

issue.title: docker-snapshot resume copies the whole writable layer with no disk preflight, no serialization and no cleanup; offer a copy-free command resume
issue.body:
## Summary

`$ --resume <id> -- <command>` on a stopped Docker container (`docker-snapshot` mode) `docker commit`s the container's **whole writable layer** to `start-command-resume/<name>:<attempt>` and runs the command in a new `<name>-resume-<attempt>` container. Nothing bounds that copy:

1. **No free-disk preflight.** The commit starts even when the data root cannot hold it. On the containerd image store (the default for fresh Docker Engine 29 installs) a commit writes a compressed blob **and** an unpacked snapshot, while the original container stays on disk. Peak usage is about 3× the writable layer.
2. **No serialization.** `$ --resume` processes for different executions commit at the same time.
3. **No cleanup.** After the new container starts, the stopped original (all of its data is now in the image) is kept, and the `start-command-resume/*` image is never removed, even after the resumed container finishes and is removed.
4. **No copy-free way to run a different command in the same container.** `docker-start` mode (no command) re-runs the original `Config.Cmd`; anything else is a full commit. The `docker-cleanup.js` hint "Run another command in the same container: `$ --resume <id> -- <command>`" is misleading: it is a copy in a new container.

On containerd the commit is also slow regardless of the change size: the default differ (`doubleWalkDiff`) walks both full trees ([Sealos measured a 1 KB commit at 39 s and 10 GB at 847 s](https://sealos.io/blog/sealos-devbox-commit-performance-optimization/)).

## Incident

link-assistant/hive-mind#2889 (2026-10-09, start-command 0.35.4; the behaviour is unchanged in 0.36.0, Docker 29.6.1 with the containerd image store). A dockerd restart killed four Rust build containers (writable layers 11, 21.2, 23.5 and 36.8 GiB, mostly Cargo `target/`). Their supervisor resumed all four with `$ --resume <uuid> -- <command>` within a minute. Four concurrent commits used about 280 % CPU for 30+ minutes and took free disk from 52 GB to 2 GB. Two commits failed with `failed to apply diff: … no space left on device`, and the two that succeeded left 11 + 23.5 GiB originals next to their images. (The record loss seen in the same incident was #193, fixed in #196.)

## Reproduction (bounded: 2 × 256 MiB, start-command 0.36.0)

```sh
for n in snap-a snap-b; do
  $ --isolated docker --detached --session $n --image alpine:3.20 -- sh -c 'dd if=/dev/zero of=/root/big bs=1M count=256; sleep 600'
done
sleep 6; docker kill snap-a snap-b

# The supervisor resumes both killed sessions with a command at the same time
$ --resume snap-a -- sh -c 'sleep 600' &
$ --resume snap-b -- sh -c 'sleep 600' &
wait

docker images 'start-command-resume/snap-*'     # a full copy of each layer
docker ps -a --filter name=snap-                # the stopped originals are still there
docker rm -f snap-a-resume-1 snap-b-resume-1    # the resumed containers are gone, the images stay:
docker images 'start-command-resume/snap-*'
```

Actual output (Docker 29.8.0, start-command 0.36.0; [script](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/blob/issue-2889-b3cf2ad55a40/experiments/issue-2889-concurrent-snapshot-resume.sh), [log](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/blob/issue-2889-b3cf2ad55a40/docs/case-studies/issue-2889/data/concurrent-snapshot-resume-start-0.36.0.log)):

```
writable layers: /snap-a=268435456 /snap-b=268435456
snap-b: $ --resume ran from +0.95s to +6.55s
snap-a: $ --resume ran from +0.95s to +6.75s
docker events (seconds after both resumes started):
  +5.72s commit snap-b
  +6.16s commit snap-a
  +6.41s start snap-b-resume-1
  +6.62s start snap-a-resume-1
start-command-resume/snap-a:1 276MB
start-command-resume/snap-b:1 276MB
snap-a-resume-1 Up 2 seconds
snap-b-resume-1 Up 2 seconds
snap-b Exited (137) 13 seconds ago
snap-a Exited (137) 13 seconds ago
after the resumed containers are removed:
start-command-resume/snap-a:1 276MB
start-command-resume/snap-b:1 276MB
snap-b Exited (137) 15 seconds ago
snap-a Exited (137) 15 seconds ago
```

The two commits overlap completely. Nothing checked the free space first. Both originals and both images outlive the resumed containers. With the incident's layer sizes, the same sequence needs about 3 × 92.5 GiB at its peak.

(On 0.35.4 two concurrent resumes of the **same** execution both committed and the second failed only at `docker run` with a container-name conflict. The #196 launch reservation in 0.36.0 now rejects the second one: `Launch reservation failed: A different resume already reserved this execution`.)

A single resume behaves the same way (Docker 29.8.0, start-command 0.35.4, 64 MiB layer): `mode=docker-snapshot in 2511 ms; images: start-command-resume/<name>:2 74.9MB`, with the original container still present ([log](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/blob/issue-2889-b3cf2ad55a40/docs/case-studies/issue-2889/data/docker-start-handoff-experiment.log)).

## Workaround (used in hive-mind#2894)

Make the container itself accept a new command, so `docker start` (no copy) is enough. The container is created with a prefix:

```sh
h='/tmp/hive-mind-resume-command-<token>'; if [ -f "$h" ]; then exec sh "$h"; fi; <original command>
```

To run a new command in the stopped container, write it with `docker cp` (works on stopped containers), then `$ --resume <id>` **without** a command:

```sh
printf 'exec sh -c %s\n' "'echo recovered; ls /root'" > /tmp/cmd && docker cp /tmp/cmd snap-demo:/tmp/hive-mind-resume-command-<token>
$ --resume snap-demo        # mode docker-start: same container ID, same writable layer, nothing committed
```

Verified on Docker 29.8.0 with start-command 0.35.4 and 0.36.0: docker-start (643 ms on 0.35.4), the same container ID, the task's files present, and no image or `-resume-` container created. For containers that still need a snapshot, hive-mind now runs them one at a time and only with free space ≥ 2 × the writable layer + 10 GiB, and it removes the original with `docker rm` (not `-f`) after the new container starts. Images are removed with `docker rmi` when the task finishes.

## Suggested fix

1. **Copy-free command resume.** Offer a mode that runs a new command in the **same** container, e.g. `$ --resume <id> --in-place -- <command>`, or make it the default when the container was launched by start-command. Launch every detached docker container with a handoff prefix like the one above (start already uses the same `docker cp` marker technique for `--on-kill-resume` in `execution-recovery.js`). On resume, `docker cp` the command into the stopped container and `docker start` it. Fall back to `docker-snapshot` only for containers without the prefix.
2. **Preflight in `docker-snapshot`.** Before `docker commit`, read `docker inspect --size -f '{{.SizeRw}}'` and the free space of the data root (`docker info -f '{{.DockerRootDir}}'`, plus containerd's root when the containerd store is used). Refuse, or wait with a clear status, when free < 2 × SizeRw + a reserve. Report `snapshotting N GiB` in the status/log.
3. **Serialize snapshots** across `$` processes, for example with a host-wide lock file next to the execution store. Do not hold the store lock itself; see #193.
4. **Clean up.** Add an opt-in `--remove-original` (or a cleanup policy) to `docker rm` the stopped original once the snapshot container is running, and `docker rmi` the `start-command-resume/*` images when the resumed container is removed by the existing cleanup policy (`docker-cleanup.js`).
5. **Fix the hint** in `docker-cleanup.js`: "Run another command in the same container" should say that it snapshots the filesystem into a new container.

issue.title: Adopt the JavaScript-first standard from router#759: CI gate, behavior parity, build load, agent rules
issue.body:
## Problem

`link-foundation/start` keeps a JavaScript implementation (`js/`, about 16k lines) and a hand-written Rust port (`rust/`, about 21k lines). The standard in link-assistant/router#759 asks for JavaScript first, a behavior-level parity gate, Rust CI/CD gated on green JavaScript CI/CD, bounded Rust build load, and agent rules with a single push gate. The repository has none of the gate, the manifest, the generation check, the build-load settings or the agent rules. Parity is only a test-count heuristic. Main has been green since 2026-09-03, so this is about process, not a broken pipeline.

## Findings

1. **Rust CI/CD is not gated on JavaScript CI/CD.** `.github/workflows/rust.yml` and `.github/workflows/js.yml` are separate workflows. Both trigger on `push` to main and on `pull_request` (rust.yml lines 3-30). No workflow uses `workflow_run`, and no Rust job has a `needs:` on a JavaScript job. Each workflow has its own path filter (`js/**` versus `rust/**`), so a change to one language never runs the other stage. A branch can run the Rust matrix (`test` on several OS, `coverage`, `build`) while JavaScript is red or still running.
2. **Parity is a test-count heuristic, not behavior parity.** `scripts/check-test-parity.mjs` greps `it(` in `js/test` and `#[test]` / `fn test_` in `rust/`, and fails only if Rust has 10% fewer tests. It runs only in `rust.yml` (job `test-parity`, line 368). There is no parity manifest, no per-feature list with JavaScript and Rust evidence, no shared fixtures or golden tests, and no JavaScript-side job that fails when Rust changes alone.
3. **Rust is not generated from JavaScript.** `rg meta-language` finds no match in the repository. Rust is maintained by hand, so there is no regenerate-and-diff check and no list of constructs that cannot be translated yet.
4. **No Rust build-load controls.** `rust/Cargo.toml` has no `[profile.*]` section, there is no `.cargo/config.toml`, and `CARGO_INCREMENTAL`, `-j` limits and `cargo-sweep` / pruning appear nowhere in the workflows. The cache step (rust.yml lines 256 and 308, repeated in `coverage` and `build`) stores `rust/target` keyed only by `hashFiles('rust/Cargo.lock')` with a broad `restore-keys` fallback, so old artifacts carry over into each new cache and grow without a bound. There are three Rust test OS legs plus a tarpaulin coverage build, each compiling the crate separately.
5. **No agent or contributor instructions.** `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` do not exist (the Rust template ships `CONTRIBUTING.md`). Nothing describes bulk drafting sub-agents, a single push owner, or running only JavaScript checks locally.
6. **Push-per-fix waste is visible.** On recent PR branches: `issue-195-cd307f03a9cf` had 2 failed `JavaScript CI/CD`, 2 failed `Rust CI/CD` and 1 failed `Workflows` run before the merge; `issue-183-4cba24615d2f` had 2 failed JavaScript runs, 1 cancelled Rust run and 1 cancelled Security run. Across the last 300 runs, 18 are cancelled and 51 failed on non-main branches (169 succeeded). Every job uses `cancel-in-progress: true`, including on `main`, while the templates use `cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}`.
7. **No branch protection.** `gh api repos/link-foundation/start/branches/main/protection` returns "Branch not protected", so neither stage is a required check.

Verified fine, not findings: actions pinning follows `.github/zizmor.yml` policy, link check, security and workflow lint exist, main CI has been green since 2026-09-03, and no pull requests are open. There are no open issues.

## Requirements

1. Make every Rust job wait for JavaScript. Either add Rust jobs to one entry workflow with `needs:` on all JavaScript jobs, or trigger `rust.yml` only through `workflow_run` with `conclusion == 'success'` and the same `head_sha`, with no `push` or `pull_request` triggers of its own. A cancelled, skipped or failed JavaScript run must not start Rust.
2. Remove path filters that let a Rust-only change skip the JavaScript gate: the parity and translation checks must always run.
3. Add `parity/features.json` listing each feature with its JavaScript and Rust implementation and test evidence, plus a checker run by both `js.yml` and `rust.yml` that fails when one side changes without the other. Keep `check-test-parity.mjs` only as a secondary signal.
4. Add shared fixtures or golden tests that both implementations must pass for CLI parsing, isolation arguments, status output and the execution record format.
5. Generate the Rust code from JavaScript with link-foundation/meta-language, or document per construct what cannot be translated yet (with issues in meta-language). Add a regenerate-and-diff CI check, and keep hand-written Rust small and listed in the manifest.
6. Add `[profile.dev]` / `[profile.test]` settings with reduced debug info, `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` in CI, a bounded shared `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` for local use, and pruning (`cargo-sweep` or a cache key that does not restore stale artifacts). Document local limits (`-j`, memory).
7. Add `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` describing: JavaScript first, drafting sub-agents never push, one CI/CD sub-agent owns `git push`, collects all failures of the last run, pushes once and never while a run is in progress on the same commits, and runs only JavaScript checks locally by default.
8. Use `cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}` as the templates do, so runs on main are never cancelled, and use a per-branch group without cancel for the gated Rust stage.
9. Enable branch protection on `main` requiring the JavaScript and Rust stage checks.
10. Add a CI check that fails if any workflow can start Rust jobs without the JavaScript gate, and report before/after pushes per PR and cancelled/failed runs per PR.

## Related

- link-assistant/router#759 (the standard and checklist).
- link-foundation/start#193 and #195 are closed and unrelated to these findings. No open issue in this repository covers any finding.

issue.title: Containers killed by a Docker daemon restart are reported as memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)
issue.body:
## Problem

`$ --list` reports containers that were killed by a **Docker daemon restart** as memory exhaustion:

```
"exitCode": 137, "oomKilled": true,
"exitReason": "memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)",
"memoryExhaustedReason": "Docker reported State.OOMKilled=true"
```

What happened (host journal, CEST): the kernel OOM-killed the **host dockerd** (global OOM, `anon-rss:7302520kB`). systemd restarted it, and during restore dockerd force-killed every running container (`Container failed to exit within 10s of signal 15 - using the force`). Earlier that day each of these task containers had a few cgroup OOM kills of a child process (`rustc` at the container's 2.9 GiB limit) that the container survived. Docker's `State.OOMKilled` stays `true` once any OOM kill happened during the container's lifetime, so the later 137 from the daemon restart was read as a container OOM kill. A container without earlier OOM events killed in the same second (`OOMKilled=false`) got no reason at all.

## Suggested fix

- Use `OOMKilled` only together with evidence that the OOM hit the container's main process at exit time: the kernel journal `oom-kill:… task_memcg=…<container id>` naming the init/main pid near `FinishedAt`, or `memory.events` `oom_kill` changing at exit.
- Detect daemon restarts (dockerd start time after the container's `FinishedAt`, many containers finished in the same second, journal `docker.service: Main process exited`) and report e.g. `killed (docker daemon restart)`.
- [`exit-reason.js`](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/exit-reason.js#L26-L31) is where the `memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)` reason is produced.

Downstream: link-assistant/hive-mind#2892.

issue.title: $ --resume starts the new container, then fails to save the record (lock timeout), leaving it running untracked
issue.body:
## Problem

`$ --resume <uuid> -- <command>` (docker-snapshot mode, start-command 0.35.4) **started the new container and then failed to save the execution record**. The container keeps running, but start-command no longer knows about it:

```
$ --resume deb9c2e9-8234-43ef-9648-e102f5d34ebd --output-format json -- solve https://github.com/link-assistant/router/issues/728 … --resume 01a1200a-…
error: Failed to acquire lock for database write
      at save (start-command/src/lib/execution-store.js:536:17)
      at resumeExecution (start-command/src/lib/execution-resume.js:493:9)
      at handleResumeQuery (start-command/src/lib/query-commands.js:60:11)
```

Afterwards:
- `docker ps`: `eec34a2b-…-resume-1-resume-2  Up 22 minutes` (the task is working fine).
- `$ --list`: the execution still says `"sessionName": "eec34a2b-…-resume-1", "status": "executed", "exitCode": 127, "resumeCount": 1`, the previous failed attempt.
- No completion watcher was attached, so the container's exit will never be written to the execution log, and `$ --status` / `--list` report the old attempt.

It happened to two of two resumes started at the same time (router#724 and router#728) while other `$` processes (another `$ --resume` blocked in a 10-minute `docker commit`, and the hive-mind bot polling `$ --list`/`--status`) were using the store.

Consequence: anything that relies on the record to decide whether a task is running treats it as dead. An automatic recovery script re-resumed both running tasks and had to be stopped before it launched duplicate solvers.

## Root cause

- [`resumeExecution`](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/execution-resume.js#L468-L494) runs the plan's steps (`docker commit`, `docker run`) first and only then calls `store.save(updated)` (L493). A save failure throws after the container is already running.
- [`LockManager.acquire`](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/execution-store.js#L227) gives up after `LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS = 30000` ([L54](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/execution-store.js#L54)). A store lock can be held for that long while another process is busy.

## Suggested fix

1. Write the "attempt N launching, session `<new name>`" record **before** `docker run` and only finalize it afterwards, so a crash or lock failure still leaves the record pointing at the new container.
2. Retry the save with backoff (well beyond 30 s) after a launch. If it still fails, stop/remove the just-started container, or print a machine-readable error naming it so the caller can recover. Today the error hides that the launch succeeded.
3. Never hold the store lock during long operations (`docker commit`/`run`). Check every writer for that.
4. `$ --status` / `--list` could reconcile `<sessionName>-resume-*` containers that exist in Docker but not in the record.

## Workaround

Detect running containers by name family (`<original>` / `<original>-resume-…`) instead of trusting the record.

---

issue.title: Docker post-mortem omits the `Memory:` line (cgroup OOM counters) when the docker daemon is remote / Docker-in-Docker, with no reason given
issue.body:
## Summary

The `Memory:` line of the docker post-mortem (#182) is missing when `$` runs inside a container that talks to a Docker-in-Docker daemon (the Hive Mind Telegram bot setup), even though the task container's cgroup recorded 13 OOM events. Nothing in the log explains why it is missing, so the post-mortem does not say that the container hit its own memory limit.

## Evidence (link-assistant/hive-mind#2803, start-command 0.35.4)

The post-mortem written by `$`:

```
=== Container post-mortem ===
Container:  05b20a82-4262-46ec-b26e-26adf5accf65
Exit Code:  1
OOMKilled:  true
StartedAt:  2026-10-08T12:11:55.544023396Z
FinishedAt: 2026-10-08T13:21:56.743898681Z
Lifetime:   4201.199s
Error:      (none)
```

Inside the same container, the cgroup showed (as read by Hive Mind from the container itself):

```
431 MB used, 2.9 GB limit, peak 2.9 GB, 3 process(es) killed by the OOM killer, memory.events oom=13
```

## Root cause (from src/lib/cgroup-memory.js)

`__start_command_cgroup_dir` finds the cgroup through `/proc/<State.Pid>/cgroup` and then `/sys/fs/cgroup/{system.slice/docker-<id>.scope,docker/<id>}` on the machine where `$` runs. With a dind or remote daemon, `State.Pid` belongs to the daemon's PID namespace and those paths do not exist on the caller, so the sampler exits quietly (`|| exit 0`) and no sample is ever written. The file header calls this best effort, but the post-mortem gives no sign that the counters are unknown.

## Reproduction

```bash
docker run -d --privileged --name dind -e DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR= docker:dind
docker run --rm -it --link dind -e DOCKER_HOST=tcp://dind:2375 oven/bun sh -c '
  apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq docker.io >/dev/null && bun add -g start-command &&
  $ --isolated docker --image alpine --detached --session m -- sh -c "sleep 3; tail /dev/zero" &&
  docker update --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m m
  # after the OOM kill:
  $ --status m        # no cgroup counters
  # the post-mortem has OOMKilled: true but no Memory: line
'
```

(Any setup where the docker daemon runs in another PID/mount namespace from `$` behaves the same.)

## Suggested fix

1. **Fallback through the daemon.** When no local cgroup directory is found, sample from inside the container: `docker exec <c> sh -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.peak /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events'`. With the default `cgroupns=private` the container sees its own cgroup at `/sys/fs/cgroup`. This works with remote and dind daemons. It needs a shell in the image, so skip it quietly when there is none.
2. **Always print the line.** When no sample exists, still write `Memory:     unavailable (cgroup not visible from this host: remote/dind daemon)` or the actual reason. A missing line is then distinguishable from a container with no OOM.
3. **Limit without counters.** Even without counters, `docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}'` gives the configured limit. Print it (`memory.limit=3135373312 (HostConfig)`) so the reader can compare it with the peak reported elsewhere.

## Workaround

Hive Mind samples the cgroup from inside the task container itself, and its kill diagnostics show the counters. Other callers that use `$` alone get no memory evidence in this setup.

issue.title: `--on-kill-resume` / `--resume`: allow a different (random-range) memory limit for the recovery after an OOM kill
issue.body:
## Summary

When a docker execution is resumed after an OOM kill, through `--on-kill-resume` or `$ --resume <id>`, the replacement keeps exactly the memory limit that just killed it: `docker start` keeps HostConfig, and #176 copies it into a new container. Please add a way to give the recovery a different memory limit, ideally a random range, for example:

```
--on-kill-resume-memory <size|N%|MIN%-MAX%>   limit used for the resume after an OOM kill
$ --resume <id> --memory <size|N%|MIN%-MAX%>  explicit override on a manual resume
```

## Context

In link-assistant/hive-mind#2803 a task ran under a 2.9 GB cap on an 11.7 GB host. The cgroup OOM killer took Claude (`memory.events oom=13`, `oom_kill=3`, `State.OOMKilled=true`). Hive Mind now restarts such tasks with a lower cap drawn from **70%-80%** of host RAM, while normal launches use 90%-100%. Lowering the cap on recovery is deliberate: when the host itself is short of memory, the restarted task is cut back earlier than the tasks that were not killed, so the same spike does not take every task down again. `--on-kill-resume-delay` (#181) already spreads out the restart time. This request does the same for the restart limit.

## Reproduction (start-command 0.35.4)

```bash
$ --isolated docker --image alpine --detached --session oom-demo --on-kill-resume \
  -- sh -c 'sleep 3; tail /dev/zero'      # grows until the OOM killer takes it
docker update --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m oom-demo   # cap it before it starts growing
# after the kill, --on-kill-resume restarts it:
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}' oom-demo      # → 67108864, same limit
# there is no option to make the recovery use a different limit
```

## Suggested fix

- When a resume is triggered by an OOM kill (`OOMKilled=true` together with a cgroup `oom_kill` delta, so the #178 rules still apply), resolve `--on-kill-resume-memory` and run `docker update --memory X --memory-swap X` before `docker start`. On the copy-to-new-container path, pass `--memory X` to the new `docker create` instead.
- Record the old and new limit in the attempt boundary of the log (#187), for example `Recovery memory limit: 2.9 GB → 8.6 GB (70%-80%)`.
- Store it with the execution so `--status` shows the limit actually in force.

## Workaround

Hive Mind runs `docker update` itself after `docker start` (src/session-kill-resume.in-place.lib.mjs). That leaves a short window in which the resumed command runs under the old limit, because `docker start` has already released it.

issue.title: feat: Docker resource controls and reliable execution recovery
issue.body:
Docker tasks can now receive launch and recovery resource limits, opt into delayed CPU penalties, and report memory diagnostics through remote/DinD daemons. Launch identities are saved before Docker side effects, and terminal OOM classification requires exit-time evidence rather than historical child-process kills.

This single PR implements all six issues in both JavaScript and Rust:

| Issue | Result |
| --- | --- |
| #189 | Opt-in CPU penalty with all requested flags/defaults, timestamp-weighted full windows, outage/restart resets, daemon resize handling, finite base restoration, transition logs and status. Works with attached/detached execution and disabled tracking. |
| #190 | `--memory`, `--memory-swap` and `--cpus` accept absolute values, daemon percentages and uniform random ranges. Resolve before run/create, default swap to memory, record requested/resolved values, preserve choices on plain resume and forward raw settings through JS isolation stacks. |
| #191 | `--on-kill-resume-memory` and manual resume overrides update limits before starting the command; snapshot replacements receive limits at creation. Fresh qualifying OOM recoveries draw again and log/store old/new/spec values. Ordinary exit 0/1 remains final. |
| #192 | Container-attributed local cgroups first, daemon exec fallback in private namespaces, last-good samples across outages, and an unconditional `Memory:` line with the observed unavailability reason and HostConfig limit. Missing shells do not abort execution. |
| #193 | Durable launch reservations on initial/manual/automatic paths, populated atomic lock publication, short malformed-lock grace, atomic database replacement, and no database lock across Docker work. Postlaunch save failure still attaches the watcher, attempts to stop the container and returns machine-readable identity/running state. |
| #194 | Historical `OOMKilled`/counters plus 137 now yield unknown SIGKILL. A fresh sampled delta can establish terminal OOM; Docker service journal evidence plus the exact container's force-kill line establishes daemon restart and takes precedence. Evidence survives log loss and is shared by attached diagnostics, finalization, status/list and recovery. |

The [complete numbered requirement/solution checklist](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/issue-195-cd307f03a9cf/docs/case-studies/issue-195/requirements.md) covers every issue and comment requirement. [Research and alternatives](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/issue-195-cd307f03a9cf/docs/case-studies/issue-195/research.md) evaluate Docker/cgroup semantics, Hive Mind's CPU policy, dockerode, Bollard, proper-lockfile and fs2. The implementation reuses the existing Docker CLI and shared file format without new dependencies. Existing legacy CPU period/quota configurations remain compatible with in-place updates.

[Tracking case study](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/tree/issue-195-cd307f03a9cf/docs/case-studies/issue-193) and [exit-attribution case study](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/tree/issue-195-cd307f03a9cf/docs/case-studies/issue-194) include UTC timelines, evidence versus inference, all original reports/comments, complete redacted incident archives and SHA-256 manifests. Debug tracing remains off by default. Downstream reports include reproduction, workarounds and code-fix recommendations.

Validation:

- Final-head CI on `e9cbeb4`: JavaScript, Rust, Security, Workflows and Broken Link Checker all pass. Linux/macOS/Windows platform tests and both coverage gates pass.
- JavaScript: `bun run check`; full suite with coverage, 1,112 passing tests; 89.92% line coverage exceeds the existing 45% gate.
- Rust: `cargo fmt --check`; `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --all-targets --all-features` (986 passing tests); six documentation tests.
- Test parity, all five documented examples, shared-script syntax and evidence integrity/credential scans pass. Offline CI regressions verify cached tags, mirror fallback, bounded failure, and no Alpine probes against unavailable or Windows-mode daemons.
- New regression files #189–194 in each implementation reproduce the defects and test both ordinary and failure paths. Finite shell fixtures verify CPU apply/lift/reapply with tracking disabled, remote memory sampling, missing shells, shared namespaces and outages. Lock/store tests inject malformed owner data, partial ENOSPC writes, concurrent writers, reservation failure and postlaunch persistence failure.
- Real Docker smoke tests pass for ordinary attached and detached execution in both CLIs, including final exit/status and the unconditional memory diagnostic.

Reproduction commands:

```sh
bun test ./js/test/regression-189.js ./js/test/regression-190.js ./js/test/regression-191.js ./js/test/regression-192.js ./js/test/regression-193.js ./js/test/regression-194.js
cd rust
cargo test --test regression_189 --test regression_190 --test regression_191 --test regression_192 --test regression_193 --test regression_194
```

Actual CPU/memory enforcement and main-process cgroup OOM could not be reproduced on this runner: runc rejects resource-limited containers because its cgroup is in threaded mode. The bounded real-resource probe and its complete failure output are committed. No host-wide OOM, disk-fill or live daemon restart was induced; those supplied incidents are reproduced with bounded fault/journal fixtures. issue.title: Docker isolation: launch-time `--memory` / `--memory-swap` / `--cpus`, with percentages and random ranges (`90%-100%`)
issue.body:
## Summary

`$ --isolated docker` has no launch-time resource flags (`--memory`, `--memory-swap`, `--cpus`). A caller that wants a RAM cap has to hold the command behind its own start gate, run `docker update --memory … --memory-swap …` from outside, and only then release the command. Please add these flags. They should accept absolute sizes, a percentage of host capacity, and a **random percentage range** (for example `90%-100%`) that is resolved once per launch.

## Why a random range

Hive Mind runs several AI tasks at once on one host, each in its own `$ --isolated docker --detached` container. In link-assistant/hive-mind#2803 every container had the same fixed cap: 25% of the host, which is 3135373312 bytes (2.9 GB) on an 11.7 GB host. When load rose, tasks reached that cap together. The cgroup OOM killer took Claude (exit 137) while the host still had 7.5 GB available:

```
container cgroup reading — 431 MB used, 2.9 GB limit, peak 2.9 GB, 3 process(es) killed by the OOM killer, memory.events oom=13
host memory now — 7.7 GB of 11.7 GB RAM available (33.7% used)
```

If each launch draws its limit from a range, tasks under the same load hit their caps at different moments, so one memory spike is less likely to kill every task at once. `--on-kill-resume-delay <min>-<max>` (#181) already applies the same idea to restart timing.

## Reproduction (start-command 0.35.4)

```bash
$ --isolated docker --image alpine --memory 1g -- sh -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max'
# → the flag is not recognised; there is no way to set the limit at launch

# Current workaround (what Hive Mind does in src/isolation-runner.lib.mjs):
$ --isolated docker --image alpine --detached --session demo -- sh -c 'while [ ! -e /tmp/go ]; do sleep 0.1; done; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max'
docker update --memory 1073741824 --memory-swap 1073741824 demo
docker exec demo touch /tmp/go
```

## Suggested behaviour

```
--memory <size|N%|MIN%-MAX%>       e.g. 4g, 25%, 90%-100%
--memory-swap <size|N%|MIN%-MAX%>  defaults to --memory (no extra swap)
--cpus <n|N%|MIN%-MAX%>
```

- Percentages are of the host as the docker daemon sees it (`docker info` → `MemTotal` / `NCPU`), so they also work with a remote or dind daemon.
- A range is resolved once, uniformly, when the container is created. Write the resolved bytes in the session log header (`Limits: memory=… (90%-100% → 10.9 GB)`) and in `--status`.
- Pass the limits to `docker run`/`docker create`. #176 already copies HostConfig limits on resume, so the same values survive `--resume`.
- Reject invalid input early: `100%-90%`, values above 100% or at most 0%, and bad units.

## Workaround

Keep the start gate and the outside `docker update` described above. It works, but every caller has to write its own gate, and a crash between `create` and `update` leaves the container unlimited.

issue.title: Docker isolation: optional delayed CPU penalty (cap a container that keeps all CPUs busy, lift it once it calms down)
issue.body:
## Summary

Add an **optional, delayed CPU penalty** for `$ --isolated docker` containers. When a container keeps all of its CPUs busy for a whole trigger window, cap it to a few CPUs with `docker update --cpus`. Lift the cap once it has stayed quiet for a whole release window.

Requested by [link-assistant/hive-mind#2801](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2801). Hive Mind enables this by default for its Docker tasks; for `start` it should be **opt-in**. Until `start` supports it, Hive Mind ships its own implementation in its session monitor ([link-assistant/hive-mind#2802](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2802)). Once `start` has it, Hive Mind would forward its settings to `$` and keep its own monitor only as a fallback for older `start` versions.

## Behaviour

> If any task uses all 100% of virtual machine CPUs for more than 15 minutes it should be restricted to 2 CPUs per docker container until for at least 15 minutes average CPU usage is below 65% of total CPU cores [...] from that moment we monitor for next 15 minutes, if again usage is more than total machine cores [...] for at least 15 minutes the task again will be restricted.

1. **Observing.** Sample the container's CPU usage (100% = one core). If its average over the last `trigger-window` is at least `trigger`% of the CPUs it may use, apply `docker update --cpus <penalty-cpus>`. The CPUs it may use are `docker info .NCPU`, re-read regularly because a VM can be resized, or its own `--cpus` limit when that is lower.
2. **Penalized.** Once the cap has been in place for at least `release-window` and the average over that window is below `release`% of the cap (65% of 2 CPUs = 1.3 cores), restore the base limit.
3. After a lift, observation starts from scratch: the full trigger window has to pass again before another penalty.

Skip the penalty when `penalty-cpus` is not below the container's own capacity. A 15-minute average only counts when samples cover the whole window. Samples lost during a watcher restart or a `docker stats` outage must not be treated as busy.

## Proposed CLI (mirrors Hive Mind's `--container-cpu-penalty*` options)

| Option                             | Default when enabled | Meaning                                                 |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--cpu-penalty`                    | off                  | Enable the penalty (docker isolation only)              |
| `--cpu-penalty-cpus <n>`           | `2`                  | Cap applied to a penalized container                    |
| `--cpu-penalty-trigger <p%>`       | `95%`                | Share of the container's CPUs that counts as "all CPUs" |
| `--cpu-penalty-trigger-window <d>` | `15m`                | How long the trigger average must hold                  |
| `--cpu-penalty-release <p%>`       | `65%`                | Share of the cap to stay below for a lift               |
| `--cpu-penalty-release-window <d>` | `15m`                | How long the release average must hold                  |

Durations accept `ms`/`s`/`m`/`h`. Hive Mind needs two more things:

- **`$ --status` reports the state**, for example `cpuPenalty: { phase: 'penalized', since, limitCpus: 2, baseCpus: null, penaltyCount: 1, penalizedMs }`, so a bot can show it in its completion message.
- **One log line per transition**, for example `[start] CPU penalty applied: 2 CPUs (5.9 of 6 CPUs for 15m)` and `[start] CPU penalty lifted: 6 CPUs (0.4 CPUs for 15m)`.

## Docker facts the implementation needs (verified on Docker 28, cgroup v2)

- `docker update --cpus 0` exits 0 **but keeps the old cap**. It cannot lift a penalty.
- `docker update --cpu-quota -1` lifts the cgroup cap but leaves the old `HostConfig.NanoCpus` behind.
- `docker update --cpus <NCPU>` lifts cleanly (`cpu.max 600000 100000` on a 6-CPU host). Values above NCPU are rejected (`range of CPUs is from 0.01 to 6.00`).
- `docker stats --no-stream <a> <b>` fails as a whole, with exit 1 and no output, as soon as one named container is gone. Sample all running containers and filter.
- **Interaction with `--resume` (issue #176):** `readDockerResourceLimits` copies `HostConfig.NanoCpus` into the resumed container. A container resumed while penalized therefore inherits the 2-CPU cap as if it were the base limit. The watcher should remember the base limit at launch, re-apply that on resume, and either continue the penalty phase or start observing afresh.

Experiment scripts and logs: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/tree/issue-2801-f9bf1f787e57/experiments (`issue-2801-*`).

## Suggested implementation

The detached completion watcher already outlives the CLI, so it is the natural owner. It could run a small sampling loop next to `docker logs -f`, for example every 30 s, using `docker stats --no-stream --format '{{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}'` or the container's `cpu.stat` `usage_usec` delta. The window averages are timestamp-based, so the sampling interval does not change the semantics. Hive Mind's state machine is pure and could be ported directly: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/blob/issue-2801-f9bf1f787e57/src/docker-cpu-penalty.lib.mjs (`evaluateDockerCpuPenalty`).

issue.title: feat: Docker resource controls and reliable execution recovery
issue.body:
Docker tasks can now receive launch and recovery resource limits, opt into delayed CPU penalties, and report memory diagnostics through remote/DinD daemons. Launch identities are saved before Docker side effects, and terminal OOM classification requires exit-time evidence rather than historical child-process kills.

This single PR implements all six issues in both JavaScript and Rust:

| Issue | Result |
| --- | --- |
| #189 | Opt-in CPU penalty with all requested flags/defaults, timestamp-weighted full windows, outage/restart resets, daemon resize handling, finite base restoration, transition logs and status. Works with attached/detached execution and disabled tracking. |
| #190 | `--memory`, `--memory-swap` and `--cpus` accept absolute values, daemon percentages and uniform random ranges. Resolve before run/create, default swap to memory, record requested/resolved values, preserve choices on plain resume and forward raw settings through JS isolation stacks. |
| #191 | `--on-kill-resume-memory` and manual resume overrides update limits before starting the command; snapshot replacements receive limits at creation. Fresh qualifying OOM recoveries draw again and log/store old/new/spec values. Ordinary exit 0/1 remains final. |
| #192 | Container-attributed local cgroups first, daemon exec fallback in private namespaces, last-good samples across outages, and an unconditional `Memory:` line with the observed unavailability reason and HostConfig limit. Missing shells do not abort execution. |
| #193 | Durable launch reservations on initial/manual/automatic paths, populated atomic lock publication, short malformed-lock grace, atomic database replacement, and no database lock across Docker work. Postlaunch save failure still attaches the watcher, attempts to stop the container and returns machine-readable identity/running state. |
| #194 | Historical `OOMKilled`/counters plus 137 now yield unknown SIGKILL. A fresh sampled delta can establish terminal OOM; Docker service journal evidence plus the exact container's force-kill line establishes daemon restart and takes precedence. Evidence survives log loss and is shared by attached diagnostics, finalization, status/list and recovery. |

The [complete numbered requirement/solution checklist](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/issue-195-cd307f03a9cf/docs/case-studies/issue-195/requirements.md) covers every issue and comment requirement. [Research and alternatives](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/issue-195-cd307f03a9cf/docs/case-studies/issue-195/research.md) evaluate Docker/cgroup semantics, Hive Mind's CPU policy, dockerode, Bollard, proper-lockfile and fs2. The implementation reuses the existing Docker CLI and shared file format without new dependencies. Existing legacy CPU period/quota configurations remain compatible with in-place updates.

[Tracking case study](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/tree/issue-195-cd307f03a9cf/docs/case-studies/issue-193) and [exit-attribution case study](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/tree/issue-195-cd307f03a9cf/docs/case-studies/issue-194) include UTC timelines, evidence versus inference, all original reports/comments, complete redacted incident archives and SHA-256 manifests. Debug tracing remains off by default. Downstream reports include reproduction, workarounds and code-fix recommendations.

Validation:

- Final-head CI on `e9cbeb4`: JavaScript, Rust, Security, Workflows and Broken Link Checker all pass. Linux/macOS/Windows platform tests and both coverage gates pass.
- JavaScript: `bun run check`; full suite with coverage, 1,112 passing tests; 89.92% line coverage exceeds the existing 45% gate.
- Rust: `cargo fmt --check`; `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --all-targets --all-features` (986 passing tests); six documentation tests.
- Test parity, all five documented examples, shared-script syntax and evidence integrity/credential scans pass. Offline CI regressions verify cached tags, mirror fallback, bounded failure, and no Alpine probes against unavailable or Windows-mode daemons.
- New regression files #189–194 in each implementation reproduce the defects and test both ordinary and failure paths. Finite shell fixtures verify CPU apply/lift/reapply with tracking disabled, remote memory sampling, missing shells, shared namespaces and outages. Lock/store tests inject malformed owner data, partial ENOSPC writes, concurrent writers, reservation failure and postlaunch persistence failure.
- Real Docker smoke tests pass for ordinary attached and detached execution in both CLIs, including final exit/status and the unconditional memory diagnostic.

Reproduction commands:

```sh
bun test ./js/test/regression-189.js ./js/test/regression-190.js ./js/test/regression-191.js ./js/test/regression-192.js ./js/test/regression-193.js ./js/test/regression-194.js
cd rust
cargo test --test regression_189 --test regression_190 --test regression_191 --test regression_192 --test regression_193 --test regression_194
```

All six issues are implemented; none is deferred or treated as already resolved. Actual CPU/memory enforcement and main-process cgroup OOM could not be reproduced on this runner: runc rejects resource-limited containers because its cgroup is in threaded mode. The bounded real-resource probe and its complete failure output are committed. No host-wide OOM, disk-fill or live daemon restart was induced; those supplied incidents are reproduced with bounded fault/journal fixtures. The sampled-delta option allowed by #194 provides temporal evidence, not exact main-PID proof; inaccessible journals or missing final samples yield unknown cause. See [verification and reproduction limits](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/issue-195-cd307f03a9cf/docs/case-studies/issue-195/verification.md).

[CI investigation](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/issue-195-cd307f03a9cf/docs/case-studies/issue-195/ci-investigation.md) records preserved failed-run logs and the fixes: official image preloading with bounded mirror fallback, checksum-verified native Actionlint, valid Rust action pins, Windows test portability, and correct Linux-container capability checks for the existing shell tests. Real Docker integration tests and existing quality gates remain enabled.

Includes a JavaScript minor changeset and Rust minor changelog fragment; release versions remain managed by CI.

Downstream reports: [tracking failure and storage recommendations](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2889#issuecomment-6089357064), [exit attribution and daemon workarounds](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2892#issuecomment-6089357423).

Fixes #189
Fixes #190
Fixes #191
Fixes #192
Fixes #193
Fixes #194

issue.title: $ --resume starts the new container, then fails to save the record (lock timeout), leaving it running untracked
issue.body:
## Problem

`$ --resume <uuid> -- <command>` (docker-snapshot mode, start-command 0.35.4) **started the new container and then failed to save the execution record**. The container keeps running, but start-command no longer knows about it:

```
$ --resume deb9c2e9-8234-43ef-9648-e102f5d34ebd --output-format json -- solve https://github.com/link-assistant/router/issues/728 … --resume 01a1200a-…
error: Failed to acquire lock for database write
      at save (start-command/src/lib/execution-store.js:536:17)
      at resumeExecution (start-command/src/lib/execution-resume.js:493:9)
      at handleResumeQuery (start-command/src/lib/query-commands.js:60:11)
```

Afterwards:
- `docker ps`: `eec34a2b-…-resume-1-resume-2  Up 22 minutes` (the task is working fine).
- `$ --list`: the execution still says `"sessionName": "eec34a2b-…-resume-1", "status": "executed", "exitCode": 127, "resumeCount": 1`, the previous failed attempt.
- No completion watcher was attached, so the container's exit will never be written to the execution log, and `$ --status` / `--list` report the old attempt.

It happened to two of two resumes started at the same time (router#724 and router#728) while other `$` processes (another `$ --resume` blocked in a 10-minute `docker commit`, and the hive-mind bot polling `$ --list`/`--status`) were using the store.

Consequence: anything that relies on the record to decide whether a task is running treats it as dead. An automatic recovery script re-resumed both running tasks and had to be stopped before it launched duplicate solvers.

## Root cause

- [`resumeExecution`](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/execution-resume.js#L468-L494) runs the plan's steps (`docker commit`, `docker run`) first and only then calls `store.save(updated)` (L493). A save failure throws after the container is already running.
- [`LockManager.acquire`](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/execution-store.js#L227) gives up after `LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS = 30000` ([L54](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/execution-store.js#L54)). A store lock can be held for that long while another process is busy.

## Suggested fix

1. Write the "attempt N launching, session `<new name>`" record **before** `docker run` and only finalize it afterwards, so a crash or lock failure still leaves the record pointing at the new container.
2. Retry the save with backoff (well beyond 30 s) after a launch. If it still fails, stop/remove the just-started container, or print a machine-readable error naming it so the caller can recover. Today the error hides that the launch succeeded.
3. Never hold the store lock during long operations (`docker commit`/`run`). Check every writer for that.
4. `$ --status` / `--list` could reconcile `<sessionName>-resume-*` containers that exist in Docker but not in the record.

## Workaround

Detect running containers by name family (`<original>` / `<original>-resume-…`) instead of trusting the record.

---

We need to download all logs and data related about the issue to this repository, make sure we compile that data to `./docs/case-studies/issue-{id}` folder, and use it to do deep case study analysis (also make sure to search online for additional facts and data), in which we will reconstruct timeline/sequence of events, list of each and all requirements from the issue, find root causes of the each problem, and propose possible solutions and solution plans for each requirement (we should also check known existing components/libraries, that solve similar problem or can help in solutions).

If there is not enough data to find actual root cause, add debug output and verbose mode if not present, that will allow us to find root cause on next iteration.

If issue related to any other repository/project, where we can report issues on GitHub, please do so. Each issue must contain reproducible examples, workarounds and suggestions for fix the issue in code. Also double check to fully apply requirements to entire codebase, so if we have issue in multiple places, it should be fixed in all them.

Please plan and execute everything in this single pull request, you have unlimited time and context, as context auto-compacts and you can continue indefinitely, until it is each and every requirement fully addressed, and everything is totally done.

comment.body:
## Root cause found: a 0-byte `executions.lock` left by ENOSPC is never treated as stale, so every write fails forever

All four `$ --resume` runs on this host failed the same way, and so did every other write since 14:32 UTC. The cause is not contention.

```
$ ls -la ~/.start-command/          # inside the hive-mind root container, 16:25 UTC
-rw-r--r-- 1 box box 248912 Oct  9 14:27 executions.lino     ← last successful write
-rw-r--r-- 1 box box      0 Oct  9 14:32 executions.lock     ← empty, never removed
```
The disk was full at 14:32 UTC (concurrent `docker commit` snapshots, link-assistant/hive-mind#2889). The kernel logged `No space left on device` in that window.

`js/src/lib/execution-store.js` → `LockManager`:

1. `acquire()` creates the lock with `fs.writeFileSync(lockFilePath, JSON.stringify(lockData), { flag: 'wx' })`. On ENOSPC the file is **created** but its content is not written. The error is not `EEXIST`, so it is rethrown with `lockAcquired = false`, and `release()` does not unlink the file.
2. From then on, every `acquire()` sees the file and calls `readLockFile()`. `JSON.parse('')` throws, so it returns `null`.
3. `if (lockData && this.isLockStale(lockData))` → `lockData` is `null`, so the stale check (which would return `true` for `!lockData`) is **never called**, and the file is never removed.
4. `writeFileSync(..., {flag:'wx'})` → `EEXIST` → retry for `LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS` (30 s) → `Failed to acquire lock for database write`.

The same happens if the process is killed between creating and writing the file, or if the content is truncated.

Consequences seen here: `$ --resume` launched the container, then `store.save(updated)` threw. The record stayed `executed 137/127`, and **no completion watcher was started**, so the task's end will not be recorded either. `$ --status` reports these running tasks as finished. hive-mind's `/limits` and queue throttling rely on that (link-assistant/hive-mind issue to follow), and so does any `$ --list`-based recovery.

### Suggested fix

- In `acquire()`, treat an unreadable or empty lock as stale once it is older than a short grace period (for example, file `mtime` older than 2–5 s). Replace `if (lockData && this.isLockStale(lockData))` with `if (this.isLockStale(lockData, stat))`, and use `mtime` when there is no timestamp.
- Create the lock atomically with its content: write `executions.lock.<pid>.<rand>` first, then `fs.linkSync(tmp, lockFilePath)` (fails with `EEXIST` like `wx`) and unlink the temp file. A lock file then either has full content or does not exist. On any error after creation, unlink what was created.
- `$ --resume`: if saving the record fails after the container started, still start the completion watcher, retry the save, and print an explicit "running but untracked" warning with the container name (this issue's original report).
- Tests: an empty lock file, a truncated JSON lock, and an ENOSPC on write (inject `fs`) must not block later writers beyond the grace period.

Workaround: remove the empty `~/.start-command/executions.lock` (it is never a live lock once it is older than a few seconds).

<!-- hive-mind-solve-repository-mode -->

## Objective

Address every open issue listed below in [link-foundation/start](https://github.com/link-foundation/start) with a **single pull request**.

This issue was generated automatically by `/solve https://github.com/link-foundation/start` (repository mode). Native sub-issues and the complete closing-reference block below jointly define the required scope.

## Scope

- Open issues found in the repository: 6
- Issues requested in this single pull request: 6
- Issues selected for native sub-issue attachment: 6
- GitHub sub-issue limit per parent issue: 100

## Issues to address

issue.title: Containers killed by a Docker daemon restart are reported as memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)
issue.body:
## Problem

`$ --list` reports containers that were killed by a **Docker daemon restart** as memory exhaustion:

```
"exitCode": 137, "oomKilled": true,
"exitReason": "memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)",
"memoryExhaustedReason": "Docker reported State.OOMKilled=true"
```

What happened (host journal, CEST): the kernel OOM-killed the **host dockerd** (global OOM, `anon-rss:7302520kB`). systemd restarted it, and during restore dockerd force-killed every running container (`Container failed to exit within 10s of signal 15 - using the force`). Earlier that day each of these task containers had a few cgroup OOM kills of a child process (`rustc` at the container's 2.9 GiB limit) that the container survived. Docker's `State.OOMKilled` stays `true` once any OOM kill happened during the container's lifetime, so the later 137 from the daemon restart was read as a container OOM kill. A container without earlier OOM events killed in the same second (`OOMKilled=false`) got no reason at all.

## Suggested fix

- Use `OOMKilled` only together with evidence that the OOM hit the container's main process at exit time: the kernel journal `oom-kill:… task_memcg=…<container id>` naming the init/main pid near `FinishedAt`, or `memory.events` `oom_kill` changing at exit.
- Detect daemon restarts (dockerd start time after the container's `FinishedAt`, many containers finished in the same second, journal `docker.service: Main process exited`) and report e.g. `killed (docker daemon restart)`.
- [`exit-reason.js`](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/exit-reason.js#L26-L31) is where the `memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)` reason is produced.

Downstream: link-assistant/hive-mind#2892.

issue.title: $ --resume starts the new container, then fails to save the record (lock timeout), leaving it running untracked
issue.body:
## Problem

`$ --resume <uuid> -- <command>` (docker-snapshot mode, start-command 0.35.4) **started the new container and then failed to save the execution record**. The container keeps running, but start-command no longer knows about it:

```
$ --resume deb9c2e9-8234-43ef-9648-e102f5d34ebd --output-format json -- solve https://github.com/link-assistant/router/issues/728 … --resume 01a1200a-…
error: Failed to acquire lock for database write
      at save (start-command/src/lib/execution-store.js:536:17)
      at resumeExecution (start-command/src/lib/execution-resume.js:493:9)
      at handleResumeQuery (start-command/src/lib/query-commands.js:60:11)
```

Afterwards:
- `docker ps`: `eec34a2b-…-resume-1-resume-2  Up 22 minutes` (the task is working fine).
- `$ --list`: the execution still says `"sessionName": "eec34a2b-…-resume-1", "status": "executed", "exitCode": 127, "resumeCount": 1`, the previous failed attempt.
- No completion watcher was attached, so the container's exit will never be written to the execution log, and `$ --status` / `--list` report the old attempt.

It happened to two of two resumes started at the same time (router#724 and router#728) while other `$` processes (another `$ --resume` blocked in a 10-minute `docker commit`, and the hive-mind bot polling `$ --list`/`--status`) were using the store.

Consequence: anything that relies on the record to decide whether a task is running treats it as dead. An automatic recovery script re-resumed both running tasks and had to be stopped before it launched duplicate solvers.

## Root cause

- [`resumeExecution`](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/execution-resume.js#L468-L494) runs the plan's steps (`docker commit`, `docker run`) first and only then calls `store.save(updated)` (L493). A save failure throws after the container is already running.
- [`LockManager.acquire`](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/execution-store.js#L227) gives up after `LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS = 30000` ([L54](https://github.com/link-foundation/start/blob/d7e83641815cc7e8e26757f77a6f61f22924c1a7/js/src/lib/execution-store.js#L54)). A store lock can be held for that long while another process is busy.

## Suggested fix

1. Write the "attempt N launching, session `<new name>`" record **before** `docker run` and only finalize it afterwards, so a crash or lock failure still leaves the record pointing at the new container.
2. Retry the save with backoff (well beyond 30 s) after a launch. If it still fails, stop/remove the just-started container, or print a machine-readable error naming it so the caller can recover. Today the error hides that the launch succeeded.
3. Never hold the store lock during long operations (`docker commit`/`run`). Check every writer for that.
4. `$ --status` / `--list` could reconcile `<sessionName>-resume-*` containers that exist in Docker but not in the record.

## Workaround

Detect running containers by name family (`<original>` / `<original>-resume-…`) instead of trusting the record.
