issue.title: Docker post-mortem omits the `Memory:` line (cgroup OOM counters) when the docker daemon is remote / Docker-in-Docker, with no reason given
issue.body:
## Summary

The `Memory:` line of the docker post-mortem (#182) is missing when `$` runs inside a container that talks to a Docker-in-Docker daemon (the Hive Mind Telegram bot setup), even though the task container's cgroup recorded 13 OOM events. Nothing in the log explains why it is missing, so the post-mortem does not say that the container hit its own memory limit.

## Evidence (link-assistant/hive-mind#2803, start-command 0.35.4)

The post-mortem written by `$`:

```
=== Container post-mortem ===
Container:  05b20a82-4262-46ec-b26e-26adf5accf65
Exit Code:  1
OOMKilled:  true
StartedAt:  2026-10-08T12:11:55.544023396Z
FinishedAt: 2026-10-08T13:21:56.743898681Z
Lifetime:   4201.199s
Error:      (none)
```

Inside the same container, the cgroup showed (as read by Hive Mind from the container itself):

```
431 MB used, 2.9 GB limit, peak 2.9 GB, 3 process(es) killed by the OOM killer, memory.events oom=13
```

## Root cause (from src/lib/cgroup-memory.js)

`__start_command_cgroup_dir` finds the cgroup through `/proc/<State.Pid>/cgroup` and then `/sys/fs/cgroup/{system.slice/docker-<id>.scope,docker/<id>}` on the machine where `$` runs. With a dind or remote daemon, `State.Pid` belongs to the daemon's PID namespace and those paths do not exist on the caller, so the sampler exits quietly (`|| exit 0`) and no sample is ever written. The file header calls this best effort, but the post-mortem gives no sign that the counters are unknown.

## Reproduction

```bash
docker run -d --privileged --name dind -e DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR= docker:dind
docker run --rm -it --link dind -e DOCKER_HOST=tcp://dind:2375 oven/bun sh -c '
  apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq docker.io >/dev/null && bun add -g start-command &&
  $ --isolated docker --image alpine --detached --session m -- sh -c "sleep 3; tail /dev/zero" &&
  docker update --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m m
  # after the OOM kill:
  $ --status m        # no cgroup counters
  # the post-mortem has OOMKilled: true but no Memory: line
'
```

(Any setup where the docker daemon runs in another PID/mount namespace from `$` behaves the same.)

## Suggested fix

1. **Fallback through the daemon.** When no local cgroup directory is found, sample from inside the container: `docker exec <c> sh -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.peak /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events'`. With the default `cgroupns=private` the container sees its own cgroup at `/sys/fs/cgroup`. This works with remote and dind daemons. It needs a shell in the image, so skip it quietly when there is none.
2. **Always print the line.** When no sample exists, still write `Memory:     unavailable (cgroup not visible from this host: remote/dind daemon)` or the actual reason. A missing line is then distinguishable from a container with no OOM.
3. **Limit without counters.** Even without counters, `docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}'` gives the configured limit. Print it (`memory.limit=3135373312 (HostConfig)`) so the reader can compare it with the peak reported elsewhere.

## Workaround

Hive Mind samples the cgroup from inside the task container itself, and its kill diagnostics show the counters. Other callers that use `$` alone get no memory evidence in this setup.

issue.title: `--on-kill-resume` / `--resume`: allow a different (random-range) memory limit for the recovery after an OOM kill
issue.body:
## Summary

When a docker execution is resumed after an OOM kill, through `--on-kill-resume` or `$ --resume <id>`, the replacement keeps exactly the memory limit that just killed it: `docker start` keeps HostConfig, and #176 copies it into a new container. Please add a way to give the recovery a different memory limit, ideally a random range, for example:

```
--on-kill-resume-memory <size|N%|MIN%-MAX%>   limit used for the resume after an OOM kill
$ --resume <id> --memory <size|N%|MIN%-MAX%>  explicit override on a manual resume
```

## Context

In link-assistant/hive-mind#2803 a task ran under a 2.9 GB cap on an 11.7 GB host. The cgroup OOM killer took Claude (`memory.events oom=13`, `oom_kill=3`, `State.OOMKilled=true`). Hive Mind now restarts such tasks with a lower cap drawn from **70%-80%** of host RAM, while normal launches use 90%-100%. Lowering the cap on recovery is deliberate: when the host itself is short of memory, the restarted task is cut back earlier than the tasks that were not killed, so the same spike does not take every task down again. `--on-kill-resume-delay` (#181) already spreads out the restart time. This request does the same for the restart limit.

## Reproduction (start-command 0.35.4)

```bash
$ --isolated docker --image alpine --detached --session oom-demo --on-kill-resume \
  -- sh -c 'sleep 3; tail /dev/zero'      # grows until the OOM killer takes it
docker update --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m oom-demo   # cap it before it starts growing
# after the kill, --on-kill-resume restarts it:
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}' oom-demo      # → 67108864, same limit
# there is no option to make the recovery use a different limit
```

## Suggested fix

- When a resume is triggered by an OOM kill (`OOMKilled=true` together with a cgroup `oom_kill` delta, so the #178 rules still apply), resolve `--on-kill-resume-memory` and run `docker update --memory X --memory-swap X` before `docker start`. On the copy-to-new-container path, pass `--memory X` to the new `docker create` instead.
- Record the old and new limit in the attempt boundary of the log (#187), for example `Recovery memory limit: 2.9 GB → 8.6 GB (70%-80%)`.
- Store it with the execution so `--status` shows the limit actually in force.

## Workaround

Hive Mind runs `docker update` itself after `docker start` (src/session-kill-resume.in-place.lib.mjs). That leaves a short window in which the resumed command runs under the old limit, because `docker start` has already released it.

issue.title: Docker isolation: launch-time `--memory` / `--memory-swap` / `--cpus`, with percentages and random ranges (`90%-100%`)
issue.body:
## Summary

`$ --isolated docker` has no launch-time resource flags (`--memory`, `--memory-swap`, `--cpus`). A caller that wants a RAM cap has to hold the command behind its own start gate, run `docker update --memory … --memory-swap …` from outside, and only then release the command. Please add these flags. They should accept absolute sizes, a percentage of host capacity, and a **random percentage range** (for example `90%-100%`) that is resolved once per launch.

## Why a random range

Hive Mind runs several AI tasks at once on one host, each in its own `$ --isolated docker --detached` container. In link-assistant/hive-mind#2803 every container had the same fixed cap: 25% of the host, which is 3135373312 bytes (2.9 GB) on an 11.7 GB host. When load rose, tasks reached that cap together. The cgroup OOM killer took Claude (exit 137) while the host still had 7.5 GB available:

```
container cgroup reading — 431 MB used, 2.9 GB limit, peak 2.9 GB, 3 process(es) killed by the OOM killer, memory.events oom=13
host memory now — 7.7 GB of 11.7 GB RAM available (33.7% used)
```

If each launch draws its limit from a range, tasks under the same load hit their caps at different moments, so one memory spike is less likely to kill every task at once. `--on-kill-resume-delay <min>-<max>` (#181) already applies the same idea to restart timing.

## Reproduction (start-command 0.35.4)

```bash
$ --isolated docker --image alpine --memory 1g -- sh -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max'
# → the flag is not recognised; there is no way to set the limit at launch

# Current workaround (what Hive Mind does in src/isolation-runner.lib.mjs):
$ --isolated docker --image alpine --detached --session demo -- sh -c 'while [ ! -e /tmp/go ]; do sleep 0.1; done; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max'
docker update --memory 1073741824 --memory-swap 1073741824 demo
docker exec demo touch /tmp/go
```

## Suggested behaviour

```
--memory <size|N%|MIN%-MAX%>       e.g. 4g, 25%, 90%-100%
--memory-swap <size|N%|MIN%-MAX%>  defaults to --memory (no extra swap)
--cpus <n|N%|MIN%-MAX%>
```

- Percentages are of the host as the docker daemon sees it (`docker info` → `MemTotal` / `NCPU`), so they also work with a remote or dind daemon.
- A range is resolved once, uniformly, when the container is created. Write the resolved bytes in the session log header (`Limits: memory=… (90%-100% → 10.9 GB)`) and in `--status`.
- Pass the limits to `docker run`/`docker create`. #176 already copies HostConfig limits on resume, so the same values survive `--resume`.
- Reject invalid input early: `100%-90%`, values above 100% or at most 0%, and bad units.

## Workaround

Keep the start gate and the outside `docker update` described above. It works, but every caller has to write its own gate, and a crash between `create` and `update` leaves the container unlimited.

issue.title: Docker isolation: optional delayed CPU penalty (cap a container that keeps all CPUs busy, lift it once it calms down)
issue.body:
## Summary

Add an **optional, delayed CPU penalty** for `$ --isolated docker` containers. When a container keeps all of its CPUs busy for a whole trigger window, cap it to a few CPUs with `docker update --cpus`. Lift the cap once it has stayed quiet for a whole release window.

Requested by [link-assistant/hive-mind#2801](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2801). Hive Mind enables this by default for its Docker tasks; for `start` it should be **opt-in**. Until `start` supports it, Hive Mind ships its own implementation in its session monitor ([link-assistant/hive-mind#2802](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2802)). Once `start` has it, Hive Mind would forward its settings to `$` and keep its own monitor only as a fallback for older `start` versions.

## Behaviour

> If any task uses all 100% of virtual machine CPUs for more than 15 minutes it should be restricted to 2 CPUs per docker container until for at least 15 minutes average CPU usage is below 65% of total CPU cores [...] from that moment we monitor for next 15 minutes, if again usage is more than total machine cores [...] for at least 15 minutes the task again will be restricted.

1. **Observing.** Sample the container's CPU usage (100% = one core). If its average over the last `trigger-window` is at least `trigger`% of the CPUs it may use, apply `docker update --cpus <penalty-cpus>`. The CPUs it may use are `docker info .NCPU`, re-read regularly because a VM can be resized, or its own `--cpus` limit when that is lower.
2. **Penalized.** Once the cap has been in place for at least `release-window` and the average over that window is below `release`% of the cap (65% of 2 CPUs = 1.3 cores), restore the base limit.
3. After a lift, observation starts from scratch: the full trigger window has to pass again before another penalty.

Skip the penalty when `penalty-cpus` is not below the container's own capacity. A 15-minute average only counts when samples cover the whole window. Samples lost during a watcher restart or a `docker stats` outage must not be treated as busy.

## Proposed CLI (mirrors Hive Mind's `--container-cpu-penalty*` options)

| Option                             | Default when enabled | Meaning                                                 |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--cpu-penalty`                    | off                  | Enable the penalty (docker isolation only)              |
| `--cpu-penalty-cpus <n>`           | `2`                  | Cap applied to a penalized container                    |
| `--cpu-penalty-trigger <p%>`       | `95%`                | Share of the container's CPUs that counts as "all CPUs" |
| `--cpu-penalty-trigger-window <d>` | `15m`                | How long the trigger average must hold                  |
| `--cpu-penalty-release <p%>`       | `65%`                | Share of the cap to stay below for a lift               |
| `--cpu-penalty-release-window <d>` | `15m`                | How long the release average must hold                  |

Durations accept `ms`/`s`/`m`/`h`. Hive Mind needs two more things:

- **`$ --status` reports the state**, for example `cpuPenalty: { phase: 'penalized', since, limitCpus: 2, baseCpus: null, penaltyCount: 1, penalizedMs }`, so a bot can show it in its completion message.
- **One log line per transition**, for example `[start] CPU penalty applied: 2 CPUs (5.9 of 6 CPUs for 15m)` and `[start] CPU penalty lifted: 6 CPUs (0.4 CPUs for 15m)`.

## Docker facts the implementation needs (verified on Docker 28, cgroup v2)

- `docker update --cpus 0` exits 0 **but keeps the old cap**. It cannot lift a penalty.
- `docker update --cpu-quota -1` lifts the cgroup cap but leaves the old `HostConfig.NanoCpus` behind.
- `docker update --cpus <NCPU>` lifts cleanly (`cpu.max 600000 100000` on a 6-CPU host). Values above NCPU are rejected (`range of CPUs is from 0.01 to 6.00`).
- `docker stats --no-stream <a> <b>` fails as a whole, with exit 1 and no output, as soon as one named container is gone. Sample all running containers and filter.
- **Interaction with `--resume` (issue #176):** `readDockerResourceLimits` copies `HostConfig.NanoCpus` into the resumed container. A container resumed while penalized therefore inherits the 2-CPU cap as if it were the base limit. The watcher should remember the base limit at launch, re-apply that on resume, and either continue the penalty phase or start observing afresh.

Experiment scripts and logs: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/tree/issue-2801-f9bf1f787e57/experiments (`issue-2801-*`).

## Suggested implementation

The detached completion watcher already outlives the CLI, so it is the natural owner. It could run a small sampling loop next to `docker logs -f`, for example every 30 s, using `docker stats --no-stream --format '{{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}'` or the container's `cpu.stat` `usage_usec` delta. The window averages are timestamp-based, so the sampling interval does not change the semantics. Hive Mind's state machine is pure and could be ported directly: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/blob/issue-2801-f9bf1f787e57/src/docker-cpu-penalty.lib.mjs (`evaluateDockerCpuPenalty`).

issue.title: fix: scope explicit resume evidence and lifecycle to execution attempts (#187)
issue.body:
In 0.35.3, explicitly resuming a killed detached Docker execution retained its previous memory evidence and let status reuse the old exit footer while the new run was quiet. This change preserves that evidence in `attemptHistory`, resets all terminal fields, and reads current log evidence only from a byte boundary captured before launch.

Fixes #187.

JavaScript and Rust now expose the same `attempt` metadata in status/list: number, start time, log byte offset, resume mode, previous/current container names, launch acceptance, watcher attachment and last observed command output. Structured `[Start Command Lifecycle]` JSON entries report resume, accepted/failed launch, attached/failed watcher and terminal result. Launch acceptance and output are separate observations; neither asserts task progress or successful completion.

The executing record is saved before attaching the watcher, including for a relaunch. Attachment metadata merges under the database lock so an immediately completed watcher cannot be overwritten. Watchers filter Docker output using the pre-launch time, capture its timestamps with bounded streaming state, and carry an attempt identity into finalization. Automatic recovery after an explicit resume also advances the attempt and archives its evidence. Existing recovery budgets, resource limits, cleanup policies and session identity remain available.

To reproduce without Docker or memory pressure:

```sh
node --max-old-space-size=128 experiments/issue-187-resume-state.mjs
```

The script calls the actual exported `resumeExecution()` using a stored exit-137/memory-exhausted record, an old standard footer, a stopped probe, mocked successful launch and a no-op watcher. It prints the quiet current attempt, archived evidence and lifecycle events. Before the fix, the new regression failed because the record retained memory evidence, status reused the old footer, and the watcher saw the old terminal state. Both JavaScript and Rust reproductions were run before implementation.

Validation:

- Full JavaScript suite: 1,071 tests passed; coverage, ESLint, Prettier and file size checks passed.
- Full Rust suite and doctests; Clippy with warnings denied and rustfmt; release build.
- Issue-187 regressions for quiet status/list, byte boundaries, evidence reset/history, snapshot/relaunch, rejected launch/attachment, immediate completion, stale finalizers, output without a newline, log truncation, automatic recovery and real watcher-shell capture/finalization.
- Documented examples for both implementations, shared script syntax and test-count parity.
- All four GitHub Actions workflows passed for final commit `6dd64a3`, including JavaScript/Rust tests on Linux, macOS and Windows, coverage, security and link checks.

Compatibility: old records deserialize without attempt metadata, and historical byte boundaries that were never recorded stay `null`. Unreadable current logs supply no inferred log evidence. Resumed Docker logs retain their timestamp prefixes; `lastOutputAt` stays `null` until fresh command output is observed. The existing POSIX watcher requirement is unchanged. JavaScript changeset and Rust changelog fragment request patch releases.

issue.title: Explicit resume retains prior memory evidence and lacks an attempt log boundary (0.35.3)
issue.body:
Explicit `$ --resume` in start-command **0.35.3** needs attempt-scoped terminal evidence and lifecycle metadata. This surfaced while investigating [hive-mind#2498](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2498) and [PR #2499](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2499): a live resumed task can share a log whose latest exit footer still belongs to its previous killed attempt.

A finite reproduction calls the actual exported `resumeExecution()` with a stored detached Docker execution, a stopped-container probe, a successful mocked `docker start`, and a no-op watcher. No containers, OOM pressure or unbounded inputs are needed. The original record has exit 137, `memoryExhausted=true`, `memoryExhaustedReason=cgroup-oom-killer` and `cgroupMemory.oomKills=1`; its log has a standard finished/exit-137 footer.

Observed after successful resume:

- The saved record becomes `status=executing`, `exitCode=null`, `endTime=null`, and clears `exitReason` and `oomKilled`.
- **It retains `memoryExhausted`, `memoryExhaustedReason` and `cgroupMemory` from the stopped attempt.**
- `options.resumedAt` and `resumeCount` change, but the same UUID/log remain and there is **no explicit-resume attempt boundary in the log** (a resource-limit line is appended only when limits exist). Until new output/completion, the latest footer remains the previous exit 137.

`src/lib/execution-resume.js:applyResumeToRecord()` clears only part of the terminal evidence. `resumeExecution()` starts the completion watcher with the existing log before saving the resumed record. Native automatic recovery already clears `cgroupMemory` in `execution-recovery.js`, so the explicit path differs.

Please preserve previous evidence in attempt history, clear or baseline all attempt-local memory fields, and expose the current attempt's start time and log byte boundary in status/list. Append a structured lifecycle boundary for explicit resume, including attempt number, previous/new container names, accepted launch, watcher attachment and later terminal result. Launch acceptance should remain distinct from observed command output or successful completion. A last-output timestamp would also let supervisors report a quiet pending run without claiming task progress.

Hive Mind is adding its own pre-launch byte boundary, fresh attempt time, cache reset, lifecycle reporting and bounded activity reads. This protects new resumes but cannot supply upstream metadata for another client or reconstruct every older resumed record.

Reproduction script and captured JSON will be committed at:

- [experiments/issue-2498-start-resume-state.mjs](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/blob/issue-2498-69233edb3b6c/experiments/issue-2498-start-resume-state.mjs)
- [start-0.35.3-resume-state.json](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/blob/issue-2498-69233edb3b6c/docs/case-studies/issue-2498/start-0.35.3-resume-state.json)

Run with an unpacked npm package with dependencies installed:

```sh
node --max-old-space-size=128 experiments/issue-2498-start-resume-state.mjs /absolute/path/to/start-command/package
```

Related: #180 and #182 fixed initial OOM attribution/collection; this report concerns resetting and scoping that evidence on explicit resume. #185/#186 fixed count interpretation and are consumed in 0.35.3.

issue.title: fix: keep cgroup OOM scope unknown without attributed evidence (#185)
issue.body:
Fixes #185.

`memory.events oom` counts allocation events while `oom_kill` counts killed processes. Comparing them incorrectly labeled a sample with `oom=1, oom_kill=3` as `host-or-parent`, even though a container group OOM can produce it. Equal or larger allocation counts also cannot prove container scope, and missing allocation counts cannot be treated as zero.

JavaScript and Rust now return `unknown` for counter-only OOM scope and show `OOM kill scope unknown` in status, watcher post-mortems, and recovery logs. Zero or unavailable kill counts still produce no scope note. Raw `cgroupMemory` fields, sampling, recovery history, and the exit-code guard remain intact: earlier child OOM kills cannot explain ordinary exits or other signals. Existing scope names remain available, but these counters never select them. Scope attribution requires separate kernel/cgroup evidence; collecting that evidence is outside this fix.

Updated the README and usage guide, and added patch-release changeset/changelog fragments for both implementations.

### Safe reproduction

From the repository root; no OOM or Docker daemon is needed:

```sh
node -e 'const c = require("./js/src/lib/cgroup-memory.js"); const m = c.parseCgroupMemorySample("3135373312 3135373312 1 3"); console.log(m, c.describeCgroupOomScope(m), c.formatCgroupMemory(m));'
```

Before: `host-or-parent`. After: `unknown`, with unchanged raw counters and an `OOM kill scope unknown` note.

### Regression coverage

`js/test/regression-185.js` and `rust/tests/regression_185.rs` reproduce the issue using finite synthetic samples. They cover group kills, equal counts, earlier allocation failures, zero/missing allocation counts, zero/missing kill counts, actual POSIX shell output, and the exit-code guard. Before the fix, scope/formatting assertions failed in both implementations; after the fix they pass. Existing #182 sampler/finalizer/recovery tests were updated for the conservative note.

issue.title: OOM scope inference compares process counts with allocation events
issue.body:
# OOM scope cannot be inferred by comparing `oom_kill` with `oom`

Filed as https://github.com/link-foundation/start/issues/185.

Observed in `start-command@0.35.2`, `src/lib/cgroup-memory.js:describeCgroupOomScope()` (introduced by PR #184).

The new raw task cgroup counters are useful, but this comparison assigns a scope without enough evidence:

```js
oomKills > (oomEvents || 0) ? HOST_OR_PARENT : CONTAINER_LIMIT;
```

The [kernel documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#memory-interface-files) defines `oom` as allocation attempts reaching the limit and `oom_kill` as processes killed by any OOM killer. With `memory.oom.group=1`, a single container OOM can kill several processes. These counters have different units and are hierarchical; their ratio cannot distinguish container, parent, and host scope. Unknown `oomEvents` should also not be treated as zero for attribution.

Reproduce safely, without creating an actual OOM:

```sh
npm pack start-command@0.35.2
tar xzf start-command-0.35.2.tgz
node -e 'const c = require("./package/src/lib/cgroup-memory.js"); const m = c.parseCgroupMemorySample("3135373312 3135373312 1 3"); console.log(m, c.describeCgroupOomScope(m));'
```

The result is `host-or-parent`, although that sample is compatible with a container group OOM. The inverse comparison also does not prove container scope: earlier limit-related allocation failures can coexist with a later host OOM kill.

Suggested fix: retain raw counters and describe scope as unknown unless separately attributed kernel/cgroup evidence establishes it. Exposing `oom_group_kill` and `memory.events.local` would add useful context but still requires care when attributing the final exit. Keep the 0.35.2 exit-code guard that prevents an earlier child OOM from explaining ordinary exits or other signals.

Workaround in Hive Mind PR #2499: retain `cgroupMemory` from status/list, report process counts and the raw `memory.events oom` count separately, and do not derive scope from their ratio. Keep bot-cgroup counters and uncorrelated host OOM victims as context rather than task evidence. A complete bounded probe is in `experiments/issue-2498-start-command-contract.cjs`.

release.name: [Rust] 0.22.2
release.body:
Stop reporting `exitReason: memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)` and `memoryExhausted: true` (`Docker reported State.OOMKilled=true`) for executions that exited 0, 1 or any other ordinary code while Docker's sticky `OOMKilled` flag was set. The flag is container-wide (moby/moby#43564): it turns on when *any* process in the container is OOM-killed, such as a `rustc` child under `cargo test`, and stays on until the next start. It now counts as the exit reason only when the command itself died by SIGKILL (exit 137) or its exit code is unknown, the same rule `--on-kill-resume` uses since #178. `oomKilled: true` is still reported. A stale cgroup reason stored by an older version is dropped by `--status`. An attached container kept after a child OOM kill now says `Docker reports a process in it was OOM-killed`.

Add `--on-kill-resume-delay <min[-max]>` for `--on-kill-resume`/`--recovery-command`: wait a uniformly random number of seconds (e.g. `30-90`; one number is a fixed delay, the default `0` resumes at once) before each recovery, so executions killed by the same host-wide OOM event do not all restart in the same second and trigger the next one. The chosen delay is printed in the `[Recovery k/N]` line, stored as `delayMs` in `recoveryHistory` and as `lastRecoveryDelayMs`, and shown in the `[Isolation] On kill:` line. A `--stop` or `--terminate` during the wait cancels the pending resume; `--terminate` of the already exited container now reports `recovery-cancelled` instead of failing.

Record the container's cgroup v2 memory counters for detached Docker executions: the completion watcher samples `memory.max`, `memory.peak` and the `memory.events` `oom`/`oom_kill` counters every second (and once more after the container exits, since the cgroup disappears with it). They are written as a `Memory:` line after the container post-mortem, stored as `cgroupMemory` (`limitBytes`, `peakBytes`, `oomEvents`, `oomKills`) and shown by `--status` as `Cgroup Memory:` with a note telling a container-limit OOM (`oom_kill == oom`) from a host-wide or parent-cgroup OOM (`oom_kill > oom`). A non-zero `oomKills` explains a SIGKILL or unknown exit as a cgroup OOM kill, and each `--on-kill-resume` `recoveryHistory` entry notes `oomEvents`/`oomKills` of the killed run. Hosts without cgroup v2 or with a remote `DOCKER_HOST` record nothing.

---

issue.body:
## Summary

This PR resolves all three open issues covered by #183, in **both** the JavaScript and the Rust implementation. Each issue has its own commits, regression tests and changelog entries (`rust/changelog.d/18N.md`; one combined `js/.changeset/issue-183.md`, since JS CI allows exactly one changeset per PR).

Fixes #183

Fixes #180
Fixes #181
Fixes #182

---

## #180: the sticky `OOMKilled` flag no longer explains an ordinary exit

**Root cause.** `resolveExitReason` / `resolveMemoryExhaustion` treated Docker's `State.OOMKilled=true` as the cause of *any* non-zero exit. That flag is container-wide and sticky ([moby/moby#43564](https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/43564)): it turns on when *any* process in the container is OOM-killed and stays on until the next start. **Root cause.** `State.OOMKilled` is a single sticky boolean. It cannot say:

- whether the container hit its own `--memory` limit or the host or a parent cgroup ran out of memory;
- how close the run came to its limit.

issue.title: Docker isolation: report the container cgroup OOM counters (`memory.events` oom / oom_kill) and peak memory in `--status`
issue.body:
## Problem

Docker's `State.OOMKilled` is container-wide and sticky (moby/moby#43564). It says *that* some process in the container was OOM-killed at some point, but not:

1. **how many** processes were killed (one OOM event often kills several: in link-foundation/meta-language#196 three `formal-ai-corpus-memory` children were each `Killed` with exit 137 within one `bash` loop);
2. whether the container hit **its own** `--memory` limit or the whole **host** ran out of memory and the global OOM killer picked a process in this container;
3. how close the execution came to its limit (peak usage).

The kernel already keeps all three per cgroup in [cgroup v2](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#memory-interface-files):

- `memory.events` `oom` — the cgroup hit its own limit and allocation failed;
- `memory.events` `oom_kill` — processes in the cgroup killed by **any** OOM killer, so `oom_kill > oom` points to a host-wide OOM;
- `memory.peak` / `memory.max` — peak usage and limit.

The cgroup is removed when the container stops, so these values cannot be read afterwards with `docker inspect`. `$ --status` therefore has nothing to report today, and callers fall back to the sticky flag. That is how #180 happened.

## Proposal

While a detached Docker execution runs, have the watcher sample the container's cgroup (`/sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope/` or the path from `docker inspect` `.HostConfig.CgroupParent`). It already polls the container. Store the last values in the execution record, and report them in `--status` and the post-mortem:

```
cgroupMemory: { limitBytes, peakBytes, oomEvents, oomKills }
```

With these values `memoryExhausted` can also be decided properly (#180): `oomKills > 0` combined with a main-process exit of 137 means the main process was a casualty. `oomKills > 0` with exit 0/1 means only children were killed.

## Context

hive-mind now records the same counters from *inside* the task (link-assistant/hive-mind#2498, PR #2499), but that only works while solve is alive to write a snapshot. The watcher is the one component that sees the whole lifetime of the container.

## Environment

start-command 0.35.1 (JS), Docker isolation, cgroup v2 host.

issue.title: `--on-kill-resume`: add a random delay before each recovery so executions killed by one OOM event do not all restart at the same moment
issue.body:
## Problem

`--on-kill-resume <N>` (0.35.0, #176) restarts a killed detached Docker execution right after the watcher sees it end. When one host-wide out-of-memory event kills several executions at once (several containers on the same host, each capped at a share of host RAM), every watcher resumes its container in the same second. All recoveries then rebuild their working sets at once — compilers, test runners, language servers — and can trigger the next OOM event immediately.

This was raised for hive-mind in link-assistant/hive-mind#2498 ([owner feedback](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2499)): "on recovery from out of memory … we don't do it all at the same time and have some random interval from 30 to 90 seconds". hive-mind now waits a random 30–90 s before each of its own recoveries (`--session-kill-resume-delay`, default `30-90`, `0` disables), but executions that rely on `$ --on-kill-resume` have no equivalent.

## Proposal

- Add `--on-kill-resume-delay <min[-max]>` (seconds). Before each recovery attempt the watcher waits a uniformly random delay in that range. A single number means a fixed delay, `0` means no delay.
- Print the chosen delay in the `[Recovery k/N]` line and store it in `recoveryHistory` (e.g. `delayMs`), so a post-mortem can see that recoveries were spread out.
- `--stop` during the wait cancels the pending recovery, as it already does for later attempts.

A default of `0` keeps the current behaviour. Callers that run many executions on one host can opt in with e.g. `30-90`.

## Environment

start-command 0.35.1 (JS), Docker isolation, detached mode.

issue.title: `$ --status` reports `memoryExhausted` / `exitReason: memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)` for an ordinary exit 0/1 when the sticky `OOMKilled` flag is set
issue.body:
## Summary

`resolveExitReason()` and `resolveMemoryExhaustion()` in `js/src/lib/exit-reason.js` (start-command 0.35.1, still on `main`) treat Docker's `State.OOMKilled` as proof that **the command** ran out of memory, whatever its exit code. Since moby/moby#43564, that flag is container-wide and sticky: it is set as soon as **any** process in the container cgroup is OOM-killed, and it is cleared only when the container starts again.

So when a child process (here a `rustc` inside `cargo test`) is OOM-killed, and the main command keeps running and later exits `1` for an unrelated reason, `$ --status` reports:

```
exitCode 1
oomKilled true
exitReason memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)
memoryExhausted true
memoryExhaustedReason Docker reported State.OOMKilled=true
```

Consumers then show "memory exhaustion" as the reason the command exited. In link-assistant/hive-mind#2498, the command actually stopped about 8 minutes after the OOM event because a Claude OAuth session expired. The pull request still got a notice saying `$ --status reports memory exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)`.

#178 fixed the same assumption in `isKilledExit()` / `--on-kill-resume`. These two functions were not changed.

## Reproduction

```js
// npm pack start-command@0.35.1 && tar xzf start-command-0.35.1.tgz
const { resolveExitReason, resolveMemoryExhaustion } = require('./package/src/lib/exit-reason.js');
for (const [exitCode, oomKilled] of [[0, true], [1, true], [1, false], [137, true], [137, false]]) {
  console.log(exitCode, oomKilled, resolveExitReason({ exitCode, oomKilled }), JSON.stringify(resolveMemoryExhaustion({ exitCode, oomKilled })));
}
```

Output:

```
exit=0 oomKilled=true -> exitReason="memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)" memory=null
exit=1 oomKilled=true -> exitReason="memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)" memory={"memoryExhausted":true,"memoryExhaustedReason":"Docker reported State.OOMKilled=true"}
exit=1 oomKilled=false -> exitReason=null memory=null
exit=137 oomKilled=true -> exitReason="memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)" memory={...}
exit=137 oomKilled=false -> exitReason="signal (SIGKILL)" memory=null
```

Real-world container footer (full log: https://gist.githubusercontent.com/konard/e653eed6994482185e30cf4fc6803272/raw/a2e204b9e3ba9a58014f12872bc0e2015f6a8f22/tmp-start-command-logs-isolation-docker-d9c55596-ba34-4d9a-bd29-a3403c2c191f.log.txt):

```
Exit Code:  1
OOMKilled:  true
Reason: exitCode=1 oomKilled=true
```

The log shows `(signal: 9, SIGKILL: kill)` for a `rustc` child at 19:38, then `Failed to authenticate: OAuth session expired and could not be refreshed` at 19:40, then exit 1 at 19:41.

## Expected

The sticky flag alone should count as memory exhaustion of the command only when the command itself died by a signal: exit code 137 (`128 + SIGKILL`), or, more generally, `>= 128` / a signal exit. Same rule as `isKilledExit()` after #178. For an ordinary exit (`0`, `1`, `2`, …), `oomKilled` should stay a separate observation ("a process in the container was OOM-killed"), not the exit reason.

## Suggested fix

```js
// resolveExitReason
if (input.oomKilled === true && signalNameForExitCode(input.exitCode) === 'SIGKILL') {
  return 'memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)';
}

// resolveMemoryExhaustion
if (input.oomKilled === true && signalNameForExitCode(exitCode) === 'SIGKILL') {
  return { memoryExhausted: true, memoryExhaustedReason: 'Docker reported State.OOMKilled=true' };
}
```

Log-marker detection (`detectMemoryMarker` / `detectExitReason`) can stay as it is: those markers are evidence written by the command itself. Optionally, add a separate field such as `oomEventInContainer: true` (or keep relying on `oomKilled`) so consumers can still warn that a child process was OOM-killed.

## Workaround (consumer side)

hive-mind (link-assistant/hive-mind#2498) recognises `memoryExhaustedReason === 'Docker reported State.OOMKilled=true'`, and `exitReason === 'memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)'` without a reason, as a restatement of the sticky flag. It folds them into its own `oomKilled` handling and does not report them as independent evidence of memory exhaustion.

## References

- moby/moby#43564: "A container's `State.OOMKilled` flag is now set to true immediately upon any container process getting OOM-killed by the kernel, and cleared to false when the container is restarted"
- #178: same root cause in `--on-kill-resume`
- link-assistant/hive-mind#2498: the incident and case study

issue.title: fix: sticky OOMKilled exit reason (#180), --on-kill-resume-delay (#181), cgroup v2 memory counters (#182)
issue.body:
## Summary

This PR resolves all three open issues covered by #183, in **both** the JavaScript and the Rust implementation. Each issue has its own commits, regression tests and changelog entries (`rust/changelog.d/18N.md`; one combined `js/.changeset/issue-183.md`, since JS CI allows exactly one changeset per PR).

Fixes #183

Fixes #180
Fixes #181
Fixes #182

---

## #180: the sticky `OOMKilled` flag no longer explains an ordinary exit

**Root cause.** `resolveExitReason` / `resolveMemoryExhaustion` treated Docker's `State.OOMKilled=true` as the cause of *any* non-zero exit. That flag is container-wide and sticky ([moby/moby#43564](https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/43564)): it turns on when *any* process in the container is OOM-killed and stays on until the next start. So a `cargo test` whose `rustc` child was OOM-killed, and which later exited `1` on its own, was reported as `memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)`.

**Fix.**
- A new `isOomKillOfCommand` / `is_oom_kill_of_command` applies the rule `--on-kill-resume` already uses since #178: the flag explains the exit only when the exit is 137 (SIGKILL; the OOM killer always sends SIGKILL) or the exit code is unknown.
- `oomKilled: true` is still reported as an observation.
- A stale cgroup reason stored by an older version is dropped when `--status` reads it.
- When an attached container is kept after a child was OOM-killed, the message now says "Docker reports a process in it was OOM-killed".

**Tests:** `js/test/regression-180.js`, `rust/tests/regression_180.rs`, `experiments/issue-180-sticky-oom-exit-reason.sh`.

## #181: `--on-kill-resume-delay <min[-max]>`

**What it does.**
- The recovery step waits a uniformly random number of seconds before each resume (`30-90`; a single number gives a fixed delay; the default `0` resumes at once, which keeps the current behaviour).
- The chosen delay is printed in the `[Recovery k/N]` line, and stored as `delayMs` in `recoveryHistory` and as `lastRecoveryDelayMs`. It also appears in the `[Isolation] On kill:` line and in `--status`.
- The wait runs in 1-second steps and re-reads `stopRequestedAt` before each step. A `--stop` or `--terminate` during the wait therefore cancels the pending resume.
- `--terminate` of the already-exited container now reports `recovery-cancelled` instead of failing on "is not running".
- Code: `recovery-delay.js` / `recovery_delay.rs`.

**Tests:** `js/test/regression-181.js`, `rust/tests/regression_181.rs`, `experiments/issue-181-sync-sleep.js`.

## #182: per-run cgroup v2 memory counters

**Root cause.** `State.OOMKilled` is a single sticky boolean. It cannot say:
- how many processes were OOM-killed in *this* run;
- whether the container hit its own `--memory` limit or the host or a parent cgroup ran out of memory;
- how close the run came to its limit.

The kernel tracks all of this per cgroup ([cgroup v2 docs](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#memory-interface-files): `memory.events` `oom`/`oom_kill`, `memory.peak`, `memory.max`). But that cgroup is deleted together with the container, so the counters have to be read while it exists.

**Fix.** The detached completion watcher starts a background sampler (`cgroup-memory.js` / `cgroup_memory.rs`):

1. **Find the cgroup.** It resolves the container's cgroup through `docker inspect` (`.Id`, `.State.Pid` → `/proc/<pid>/cgroup`). This covers the systemd and cgroupfs drivers, `--cgroup-parent` and rootless Docker. `system.slice/docker-<id>.scope` and `docker/<id>` are fallbacks. A candidate directory must contain the container ID.
2. **Sample.** Every second it writes `memory.max memory.peak oom oom_kill` atomically (via `mv`) into a temp file. When the cgroup is gone, the last good sample is kept.
3. **Final read.** After the container exits, the sampler is stopped and the cgroup is read one last time if it still exists. The counters are then used in several places:
   - **Log:** a `Memory:` line follows the post-mortem or the removal note:
     `Memory:     memory.max=268435456 memory.peak=268300000 oom=0 oom_kill=3 (oom_kill > oom: a host-wide or parent cgroup OOM killed processes here)`
   - **Record:** they are stored as `cgroupMemory` (`limitBytes`, `peakBytes`, `oomEvents`, `oomKills`). `--status` shows them as `Cgroup Memory:     peak 255.9 MiB of 256.0 MiB limit, oom 0, oom_kill 3 (...)`.
   - **Exit reason:** a non-zero `oomKills` explains a SIGKILL or unknown exit as `memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)` even when `State.OOMKilled` was not set. It follows the #180 rule, so it never explains an ordinary exit.
   - **Recovery:** with `--on-kill-resume`, the killed run's `Memory:` line is logged before `[Recovery k/N]`, the `recoveryHistory` entry gets `oomEvents=N, oomKills=M`, and `cgroupMemory` is cleared for the resumed run.
   - **Reading old or odd records:** stored values are read leniently (numeric strings, integral floats from Links Notation, nulls), so a malformed field never makes a record unreadable.

**Limitations (documented in the README):**
- Only cgroup v2 hosts and detached Docker executions are sampled.
- A cgroup v1 host or a remote `DOCKER_HOST` records nothing, because the watcher reads the local `/proc` and `/sys/fs/cgroup`.
- Kills in the last second can be missed if the cgroup disappears before the final read.
- `memory.peak` needs Linux 5.19 or newer.
- The note "host-wide or parent" (`oom_kill > oom`) is a heuristic.

**Tests:** `js/test/regression-182.js` (10) and `rust/tests/regression_182.rs` (11):
- parsing, scope and formatting;
- the order of steps in the watcher script;
- a real `sh` sampler that keeps its last sample after the cgroup is removed;
- full watcher runs against a fake `docker`, a fake cgroup tree and a fake `/proc` (`START_COMMAND_CGROUP_ROOT`, `START_COMMAND_PROC_ROOT`), for a kept container and for a removed one;
- the finalizer, `--status` text, and recovery history.

Experiments: `experiments/issue-182-cgroup-sampler.js`, `experiments/issue-182-store-roundtrip.js`.

## Checks run locally
- JS: `bun run check` (eslint, prettier, file size) passes; `npm test` gives 1045 pass, 0 fail.
- Rust: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo test` all pass.
- `node scripts/check-test-parity.mjs` passes (Rust 1030 / JS 1002).

Docs updated: `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/USAGE.md`.

issue.title: Docker isolation: report the container cgroup OOM counters (`memory.events` oom / oom_kill) and peak memory in `--status`
issue.body:
## Problem

Docker's `State.OOMKilled` is container-wide and sticky (moby/moby#43564). It says *that* some process in the container was OOM-killed at some point, but not:

1. **how many** processes were killed (one OOM event often kills several: in link-foundation/meta-language#196 three `formal-ai-corpus-memory` children were each `Killed` with exit 137 within one `bash` loop);
2. whether the container hit **its own** `--memory` limit or the whole **host** ran out of memory and the global OOM killer picked a process in this container;
3. how close the execution came to its limit (peak usage).

The kernel already keeps all three per cgroup in [cgroup v2](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#memory-interface-files):

- `memory.events` `oom` — the cgroup hit its own limit and allocation failed;
- `memory.events` `oom_kill` — processes in the cgroup killed by **any** OOM killer, so `oom_kill > oom` points to a host-wide OOM;
- `memory.peak` / `memory.max` — peak usage and limit.

The cgroup is removed when the container stops, so these values cannot be read afterwards with `docker inspect`. `$ --status` therefore has nothing to report today, and callers fall back to the sticky flag. That is how #180 happened.

## Proposal

While a detached Docker execution runs, have the watcher sample the container's cgroup (`/sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope/` or the path from `docker inspect` `.HostConfig.CgroupParent`). It already polls the container. Store the last values in the execution record, and report them in `--status` and the post-mortem:

```
cgroupMemory: { limitBytes, peakBytes, oomEvents, oomKills }
```

With these values `memoryExhausted` can also be decided properly (#180): `oomKills > 0` combined with a main-process exit of 137 means the main process was a casualty. `oomKills > 0` with exit 0/1 means only children were killed.

## Context

hive-mind now records the same counters from *inside* the task (link-assistant/hive-mind#2498, PR #2499), but that only works while solve is alive to write a snapshot. The watcher is the one component that sees the whole lifetime of the container.

## Environment

start-command 0.35.1 (JS), Docker isolation, cgroup v2 host.

issue.title: `--on-kill-resume`: add a random delay before each recovery so executions killed by one OOM event do not all restart at the same moment
issue.body:
## Problem

`--on-kill-resume <N>` (0.35.0, #176) restarts a killed detached Docker execution right after the watcher sees it end. When one host-wide out-of-memory event kills several executions at once (several containers on the same host, each capped at a share of host RAM), every watcher resumes its container in the same second. All recoveries then rebuild their working sets at once — compilers, test runners, language servers — and can trigger the next OOM event immediately.

This was raised for hive-mind in link-assistant/hive-mind#2498 ([owner feedback](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2499)): "on recovery from out of memory … we don't do it all at the same time and have some random interval from 30 to 90 seconds". hive-mind now waits a random 30–90 s before each of its own recoveries (`--session-kill-resume-delay`, default `30-90`, `0` disables), but executions that rely on `$ --on-kill-resume` have no equivalent.

## Proposal

- Add `--on-kill-resume-delay <min[-max]>` (seconds). Before each recovery attempt the watcher waits a uniformly random delay in that range. A single number means a fixed delay, `0` means no delay.
- Print the chosen delay in the `[Recovery k/N]` line and store it in `recoveryHistory` (e.g. `delayMs`), so a post-mortem can see that recoveries were spread out.
- `--stop` during the wait cancels the pending recovery, as it already does for later attempts.

A default of `0` keeps the current behaviour. Callers that run many executions on one host can opt in with e.g. `30-90`.

## Environment

start-command 0.35.1 (JS), Docker isolation, detached mode.

issue.title: `$ --status` reports `memoryExhausted` / `exitReason: memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)` for an ordinary exit 0/1 when the sticky `OOMKilled` flag is set
issue.body:
## Summary

`resolveExitReason()` and `resolveMemoryExhaustion()` in `js/src/lib/exit-reason.js` (start-command 0.35.1, still on `main`) treat Docker's `State.OOMKilled` as proof that **the command** ran out of memory, whatever its exit code. Since moby/moby#43564, that flag is container-wide and sticky: it is set as soon as **any** process in the container cgroup is OOM-killed, and it is cleared only when the container starts again.

So when a child process (here a `rustc` inside `cargo test`) is OOM-killed, and the main command keeps running and later exits `1` for an unrelated reason, `$ --status` reports:

```
exitCode 1
oomKilled true
exitReason memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)
memoryExhausted true
memoryExhaustedReason Docker reported State.OOMKilled=true
```

Consumers then show "memory exhaustion" as the reason the command exited. In link-assistant/hive-mind#2498, the command actually stopped about 8 minutes after the OOM event because a Claude OAuth session expired. The pull request still got a notice saying `$ --status reports memory exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)`.

#178 fixed the same assumption in `isKilledExit()` / `--on-kill-resume`. These two functions were not changed.

## Reproduction

```js
// npm pack start-command@0.35.1 && tar xzf start-command-0.35.1.tgz
const { resolveExitReason, resolveMemoryExhaustion } = require('./package/src/lib/exit-reason.js');
for (const [exitCode, oomKilled] of [[0, true], [1, true], [1, false], [137, true], [137, false]]) {
  console.log(exitCode, oomKilled, resolveExitReason({ exitCode, oomKilled }), JSON.stringify(resolveMemoryExhaustion({ exitCode, oomKilled })));
}
```

Output:

```
exit=0 oomKilled=true -> exitReason="memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)" memory=null
exit=1 oomKilled=true -> exitReason="memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)" memory={"memoryExhausted":true,"memoryExhaustedReason":"Docker reported State.OOMKilled=true"}
exit=1 oomKilled=false -> exitReason=null memory=null
exit=137 oomKilled=true -> exitReason="memory-exhaustion (cgroup-oom-killer)" memory={...}
exit=137 oomKilled=false -> exitReason="signal (SIGKILL)" memory=null
```


The sticky flag alone should count as memory exhaustion of the command only when the command itself died by a signal: exit code 137 (`128 + SIGKILL`), or, more generally, `>= 128` / a signal exit. if (input.oomKilled === true && signalNameForExitCode(input.exitCode) === 'SIGKILL') {

issue.title: fix: --on-kill-resume no longer resumes runs that exited 0/1 with Docker's sticky OOMKilled flag
issue.body:
Fixes #178

## Problem

`--on-kill-resume N` treated Docker's `State.OOMKilled=true` as a kill **whatever the exit code**. Docker sets that flag when *any* process in the container's cgroup is OOM-killed (a compiler, a test runner, a child `node`), and it stays set until the container is started again. A main process that survived that and later exited 0 (success) or 1 (a deliberate failure) on its own was resumed as if it had been killed (same "sticky OOMKilled" pattern as #151; seen in link-assistant/hive-mind#2408).

Both decision points had the bug, in JS and Rust:

- `isKilledExit` / `is_killed_exit`: `code === 137 || oomKilled`
- the watcher's shell condition (`buildRecoverySnippet` / `build_recovery_snippet`): `{ [ "$exit" = 137 ] || [ "$oom" = true ]; }`

## Fix

A container counts as killed only when the **main process** was:

- exit code `137` (SIGKILL), **or**
- `OOMKilled=true` **and no usable exit code**: missing, non-numeric, or the watcher's `-1` fallback when `docker inspect` fails or the container never finished.

Shell condition now:

```sh
{ [ "$exit" = 137 ] || { [ "$oom" = true ] && ! [ "$exit" -ge 0 ] 2>/dev/null; }; } && <recover>
```

Unlike the suggestion in the issue, the JS/Rust check also treats a negative code as "no exit code", not just `null`. The watcher writes `-1` when it cannot read one, and that keeps the runtime check and the shell check in agreement.

If `OOMKilled=true` comes with an exit of 0–127, the run is finalized with its real exit code. `oomKilled: true` still shows up in `--status`, the record and the post-mortem as an observation. Other `128+n` signals are still not treated as kills: `143` (SIGTERM) is what `docker stop` produces.

## Reproduce

```sh
./experiments/issue-178-sticky-oom.sh
```

Before the fix, `(0, true)` and `(1, true)` came out as `true` / `RECOVER`. After:

```
isKilledExit(137, "false") = true | watcher: RECOVER
isKilledExit(1, "true") = false | watcher: no recovery
isKilledExit(0, "true") = false | watcher: no recovery
isKilledExit(1, "false") = false | watcher: no recovery
isKilledExit(137, "true") = true | watcher: RECOVER
isKilledExit(-1, "true") = true | watcher: RECOVER
```

I did not run the full Docker scenario with a real OOM kill: it needs a host with a memory cgroup controller. The watcher tests below run the real watcher script against a fake `docker` instead.

## Tests

- `js/test/regression-178.js` and `rust/tests/regression_178.rs` (5 tests each; all 5 fail without the fix):
  - `isKilledExit` table: `(0,true)` and `(1,true)` → not killed; `(137,*)`, `(-1,true)`, `(null/'',true)` → killed
  - the watcher's shell condition, run in `/bin/sh`, matches `isKilledExit` for every case
  - `recoverKilledExecution` returns `not-killed` for exit 0/1 with `OOMKilled=true` and makes no docker calls
  - the real detached watcher, run against a fake `docker` reporting `0 true` / `1 true`, does not `docker start`, writes no `[Recovery` line, and finalizes with the real exit code and `oomKilled: true`
- The issue #176 tests that asserted the old `('0','true') → killed` behavior now check `('-1','true')`.
- Local runs: `bun run check` and `bun run test` (1008 pass); `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings`, `cargo test` all pass.

## Other changes

- README, ARCHITECTURE and code comments now explain the rule.
- Changesets: `js/.changeset/issue-178.md` (patch) and `rust/changelog.d/178.md` (patch).
- **CI (Security / NPM Audit):** a new advisory, [GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm) (`braces` stack-exhaustion DoS), was published after main's last green run. It covers every `braces` version, so an `overrides` bump (as in #177) cannot fix it. This PR upgrades the dev dependency `@changesets/cli` from `^2.31.0` to `^3.0.3`, which swaps `micromatch`/`braces` for `picomatch`. issue.title: `--on-kill-resume` resumes executions that exited 0/1 on their own when Docker's sticky `OOMKilled` flag is set (a child was OOM-killed)
issue.body:
## Summary

`--on-kill-resume N` (added in 0.35.0, #176) recovers an execution whenever Docker's `State.OOMKilled` is `true`, **whatever the exit code**. Docker sets `OOMKilled` when *any* process in the container's cgroup is OOM-killed (a test runner, a compiler, a child `node`), and the flag stays set until the container is started again. The main process can survive that, keep working, and later exit 0 (success) or 1 (a deliberate failure). With `--on-kill-resume`, both exits are treated as kills and the container is resumed.

This is the same "sticky OOMKilled" pattern as #151. Here it causes a resumed run instead of a wrong status.

## Real-world impact (hive-mind #2408)

Hive Mind has its own OOM recovery. On 2026-10-03 it hit this exact pattern (link-assistant/hive-mind#2408, follow-up comment on PR #2409):

1. A `solve` run had a child process OOM-killed at 16:55:17Z. The main process survived and continued.
2. Hours later the run stopped on purpose: `Auto-restart 5/5 - limit reached`, exit 1.
3. `$ --status` reported `exitCode: 1, oomKilled: true`. The recovery logic read that as an OOM kill and started a new run with a fresh restart budget. The task kept working in the background after it had been reported as failed.

Hive Mind now fixes this on its side: it checks the log for deliberate stop markers before treating `oomKilled` as a kill. But anyone who passes `--on-kill-resume` to `$` would hit the same bug inside start-command.

## Reproduction (start-command 0.35.0)

```sh
npm pack start-command@0.35.0 && tar xzf start-command-0.35.0.tgz && cd package
node -e "
const r = require('./src/lib/execution-recovery.js');
for (const [code, oom] of [[137, 'false'], [1, 'true'], [0, 'true'], [1, 'false'], [137, 'true']])
  console.log('isKilledExit(' + code + ', ' + JSON.stringify(oom) + ') =', r.isKilledExit(code, oom));
"
```

Output:

```
isKilledExit(137, "false") = true
isKilledExit(1, "true") = true     <- main process exited 1 on its own
isKilledExit(0, "true") = true     <- main process succeeded
isKilledExit(1, "false") = false
isKilledExit(137, "true") = true
```

The watcher's shell condition has the same problem (`buildRecoverySnippet`):

```sh
{ [ "$exit" = 137 ] || [ "$oom" = true ]; } && <recover>
```

Evaluating that condition with the watcher's variables:

```sh
for pair in "0 true" "1 true" "1 false" "137 false"; do set -- $pair
  __start_command_exit=$1 __start_command_oom=$2 sh -c '{ [ "$__start_command_exit" = 137 ] || [ "$__start_command_oom" = true ]; } && echo "exit=$__start_command_exit oom=$__start_command_oom -> RECOVER" || echo "exit=$__start_command_exit oom=$__start_command_oom -> no recovery"'
done
```

```
exit=0 oom=true -> RECOVER
exit=1 oom=true -> RECOVER
exit=1 oom=false -> no recovery
exit=137 oom=false -> RECOVER
```

A full Docker scenario that should trigger it: `$ -i docker -d --on-kill-resume 1 -- sh -c 'sleep 10; head -c 400m /dev/zero | tail; echo survived; exit 0'`, followed by `docker update --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m <container>`. `tail` is OOM-killed, the shell exits 0 and `OOMKilled` becomes `true`. *I could not run this part myself:* the Docker host in my sandbox has no memory cgroup controller (`docker update` fails with `memory.max: no such file or directory`). The two checks above are the code paths it would hit.

## Expected

A container counts as killed when the **main process** was killed:

- exit code 137 (SIGKILL), or 128+n for another fatal signal if you want to cover those, **or**
- `OOMKilled=true` **and** no usable exit code (the watcher could not read one).

When `OOMKilled=true` and the exit code is 0–127, the main process ran to completion. Report it as an OOM *event* (it is still useful in `--status` and the log separator), but do not resume.

## Suggested fix

```js
function isKilledExit(exitCode, oomKilled) {
  const described = describeExitCode(exitCode);
  if (described.code === KILLED_EXIT_CODE) return true;
  const oom = oomKilled === true || oomKilled === 'true';
  // Sticky cgroup flag: only meaningful when the main process has no exit status of its own.
  return oom && described.code === null;
}
```

…and in `buildRecoverySnippet`:

```sh
{ [ "$exit" = 137 ] || { [ "$oom" = true ] && ! [ "$exit" -ge 0 ] 2>/dev/null; }; } && <recover>   # oom only counts without a numeric exit code
```

Add tests for `(0, true)`, `(1, true)` → not killed, and `(137, *)`, `(null, true)` → killed.

## Workaround

Do not combine `--on-kill-resume` with workloads whose child processes may be OOM-killed while the main process survives. Alternatively, keep the decision with the supervisor (as Hive Mind does) and attribute a deliberate exit from the log before treating `OOMKilled` as a kill.

Refs: link-assistant/hive-mind#2408, link-assistant/hive-mind#2409, #151, #176.

issue.title: `--on-kill-resume` resumes executions that exited 0/1 on their own when Docker's sticky `OOMKilled` flag is set (a child was OOM-killed)
issue.body:
## Summary

`--on-kill-resume N` (added in 0.35.0, #176) recovers an execution whenever Docker's `State.OOMKilled` is `true`, **whatever the exit code**. Docker sets `OOMKilled` when *any* process in the container's cgroup is OOM-killed (a test runner, a compiler, a child `node`), and the flag stays set until the container is started again. The main process can survive that, keep working, and later exit 0 (success) or 1 (a deliberate failure). With `--on-kill-resume`, both exits are treated as kills and the container is resumed.

This is the same "sticky OOMKilled" pattern as #151. Here it causes a resumed run instead of a wrong status.

## Real-world impact (hive-mind #2408)

Hive Mind has its own OOM recovery. On 2026-10-03 it hit this exact pattern (link-assistant/hive-mind#2408, follow-up comment on PR #2409):

1. A `solve` run had a child process OOM-killed at 16:55:17Z. The main process survived and continued.
2. Hours later the run stopped on purpose: `Auto-restart 5/5 - limit reached`, exit 1.
3. `$ --status` reported `exitCode: 1, oomKilled: true`. The recovery logic read that as an OOM kill and started a new run with a fresh restart budget. The task kept working in the background after it had been reported as failed.

Hive Mind now fixes this on its side: it checks the log for deliberate stop markers before treating `oomKilled` as a kill. But anyone who passes `--on-kill-resume` to `$` would hit the same bug inside start-command.

## Reproduction (start-command 0.35.0)

```sh
npm pack start-command@0.35.0 && tar xzf start-command-0.35.0.tgz && cd package
node -e "
const r = require('./src/lib/execution-recovery.js');
for (const [code, oom] of [[137, 'false'], [1, 'true'], [0, 'true'], [1, 'false'], [137, 'true']])
  console.log('isKilledExit(' + code + ', ' + JSON.stringify(oom) + ') =', r.isKilledExit(code, oom));
"
```

Output:

```
isKilledExit(137, "false") = true
isKilledExit(1, "true") = true     <- main process exited 1 on its own
isKilledExit(0, "true") = true     <- main process succeeded
isKilledExit(1, "false") = false
isKilledExit(137, "true") = true
```

The watcher's shell condition has the same problem (`buildRecoverySnippet`):

```sh
{ [ "$exit" = 137 ] || [ "$oom" = true ]; } && <recover>
```

Evaluating that condition with the watcher's variables:

```sh
for pair in "0 true" "1 true" "1 false" "137 false"; do set -- $pair
  __start_command_exit=$1 __start_command_oom=$2 sh -c '{ [ "$__start_command_exit" = 137 ] || [ "$__start_command_oom" = true ]; } && echo "exit=$__start_command_exit oom=$__start_command_oom -> RECOVER" || echo "exit=$__start_command_exit oom=$__start_command_oom -> no recovery"'
done
```

```
exit=0 oom=true -> RECOVER
exit=1 oom=true -> RECOVER
exit=1 oom=false -> no recovery
exit=137 oom=false -> RECOVER
```

A full Docker scenario that should trigger it: `$ -i docker -d --on-kill-resume 1 -- sh -c 'sleep 10; head -c 400m /dev/zero | tail; echo survived; exit 0'`, followed by `docker update --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m <container>`. `tail` is OOM-killed, the shell exits 0 and `OOMKilled` becomes `true`. *I could not run this part myself:* the Docker host in my sandbox has no memory cgroup controller (`docker update` fails with `memory.max: no such file or directory`). The two checks above are the code paths it would hit.

## Expected

A container counts as killed when the **main process** was killed:

- exit code 137 (SIGKILL), or 128+n for another fatal signal if you want to cover those, **or**
- `OOMKilled=true` **and** no usable exit code (the watcher could not read one).

When `OOMKilled=true` and the exit code is 0–127, the main process ran to completion. Report it as an OOM *event* (it is still useful in `--status` and the log separator), but do not resume.

## Suggested fix

```js
function isKilledExit(exitCode, oomKilled) {
  const described = describeExitCode(exitCode);
  if (described.code === KILLED_EXIT_CODE) return true;
  const oom = oomKilled === true || oomKilled === 'true';
  // Sticky cgroup flag: only meaningful when the main process has no exit status of its own.
  return oom && described.code === null;
}
```

…and in `buildRecoverySnippet`:

```sh
{ [ "$exit" = 137 ] || { [ "$oom" = true ] && ! [ "$exit" -ge 0 ] 2>/dev/null; }; } && <recover>   # oom only counts without a numeric exit code
```

Add tests for `(0, true)`, `(1, true)` → not killed, and `(137, *)`, `(null, true)` → killed.

## Workaround

Do not combine `--on-kill-resume` with workloads whose child processes may be OOM-killed while the main process survives. Alternatively, keep the decision with the supervisor (as Hive Mind does) and attribute a deliberate exit from the log before treating `OOMKilled` as a kill.

Refs: link-assistant/hive-mind#2408, link-assistant/hive-mind#2409, #151, #176.

issue.title: Docker resume: re-apply resource limits on snapshot resume, add --on-kill-resume / --recovery-command (#176)
issue.body:
Fixes #176

## Problem

**1. `--resume <id> -- <cmd>` dropped the container's resource limits.** The snapshot resume (`DOCKER_SNAPSHOT`) runs `docker commit` and then `docker run` of a `<name>-resume-N` container. `docker commit` captures the filesystem and image config, but not HostConfig. So memory, CPU and PIDs limits did not carry over to the new container. This includes limits a supervisor applied with `docker update`, which were never in the stored launch options. Reproduced with `experiments/issue-176-docker-commit-drops-limits.sh`:

```
original: Memory=268435456 MemorySwap=268435456 NanoCpus=500000000 PidsLimit=64
resumed:  Memory=0 MemorySwap=0 NanoCpus=0 PidsLimit=<no value>
```

**2. There was no launch-time recovery.** When a detached container's main process was OOM-killed, the only way to continue was a new `$ --resume <id> -- <cmd>`. That needs an outside supervisor and starts a new container (losing problem 1's limits). There was no way to say at launch "on a kill, run this recovery command in the same container, under the same UUID and log".

## Fix (JS and Rust, same design)

### Resource limits survive a snapshot resume

- `docker-resource-limits.js` / `docker_resource_limits.rs` read the stopped container's limits with `docker inspect --format '{{json .HostConfig}}'` before the commit. They translate the non-default ones into `docker run` flags, only in combinations `docker run` accepts:
  - `--memory`, `--memory-swap` (only alongside `--memory`; `-1` is kept), `--memory-reservation`;
  - `--cpus`, or `--cpu-quota`/`--cpu-period` when `NanoCpus` is unset;
  - `--cpu-shares`, `--cpuset-cpus`, `--cpuset-mems`;
  - `--pids-limit`;
  - `--shm-size` (only when it differs from the 64m default), `--storage-opt`, `--ulimit`.
- The flags go into `docker run` for `-resume-N`. They are printed as an `[Isolation] Resource limits: ...` line, written to the log, stored as `resourceLimits` in the execution record, and included in the resume result (links notation, JSON and text). A later relaunch of a removed session re-applies the stored `resourceLimits` too.

### `--on-kill-resume <N>` / `--recovery-command <cmd>`

```bash
$ --isolated docker --detached --on-kill-resume 2 \
    --recovery-command 'agent --resume-from-checkpoint' -- agent --task build
```

- **Options.** Valid only with `--isolated docker` (as the only isolation level) and `--detached`. `--recovery-command` on its own implies one attempt. Both are stored in the record and listed in `--help`.
- **In the container.** The command is wrapped in a small `sh -c` selector. It runs the original argv unless the marker `/.start-command-recovery` exists. If it does, it runs the recovery command with `START_COMMAND_RECOVERY_ATTEMPT=<k>` exported.
- **In the completion watcher.** When the container exits with 137 or `OOMKilled=true`, a new branch runs before cleanup, footer and finalization. It hands off to the recovery step: `execution-recovery.js` in JS, `start --internal-recover-detached-docker` in Rust. The recovery step:
  - writes the post-mortem and a `[Recovery k/N]` separator into the **same log**;
  - logs the live `docker update` limits;
  - `docker cp`s the marker in and `docker start`s the **same container**, so the filesystem and HostConfig are unchanged;
  - records `recoveryAttempts`, `recoveryHistory` and `lastRecoveryAt` under the **same UUID**;
  - starts a new watcher that follows `docker logs -f --since <restart>`.

  When the attempts are used up, the watcher finalizes the run as before, with the real exit code.
- **`--stop`.** For such sessions `--stop` sets `stopRequestedAt` (and restores it if the stop fails), so a deliberate stop is never "recovered". A later `--resume` clears it.

## Reproducing

`experiments/issue-176-rust-e2e.sh [start-binary]` runs against real Docker. It launches with `--on-kill-resume 2`, applies `docker update --pids-limit 64`, then `docker kill`s the container three times. After that it applies `--memory 256m --memory-swap 256m --cpus 0.5` to the stopped container and runs a snapshot resume. Output with the Rust binary and, after the fix below, with the JS CLI:

```
running=true pids=64        # after kill 1: the same container is running again, limit intact
running=true                # after kill 2
running=false               # after kill 3: attempts used up
  exitCode 137
    resourceLimits --pids-limit=64
    recoveryAttempts 2
recovered attempt 1
recovered attempt 2
[Recovery] Not resuming: all 2 recovery attempt(s) used.
resume-1 mem=268435456 swap=268435456 cpus=500000000 pids=64
```

The real-Docker run also found a JS-only bug, fixed in 19e3cc3:
- `execution-recovery.js` ran its `main()` before `module.exports` was assigned. Its `require.main === module` block came first, and `docker-cleanup.js` requires the module back to build the next watcher.
- As a result, the container was restarted, but no watcher followed it, and the old watcher finalized the run as 137.

`experiments/issue-176-js-recovery-trace.sh` is the trace used to find it.

The host used here cannot *start* any container with a memory limit (`docker run --memory 256m alpine true` fails: `cannot enter cgroupv2 "/sys/fs/cgroup/docker" with domain controllers -- it is in threaded mode`). On this host, then, the memory/CPU part is verified on the resumed container's HostConfig (the last line above) rather than on a running process. PIDs limits are verified in both modes.

## Tests

- **JS:** `js/test/regression-176.js` has 34 tests:
  - HostConfig → flags parsing (defaults, swap rules, CPU exclusivity, shm, ulimits, storage-opt);
  - snapshot resume plans with and without `docker inspect`;
  - option parsing and validation;
  - the selector, run through a real `sh` with and without the marker;
  - recovery outcomes (resumed, attempts exhausted, stop requested, `docker cp`/`docker start` failures);
  - `--stop` marking;
  - the watcher run as a real shell against a stateful fake `docker`. This includes a new test that goes through the real `execution-recovery.js` entry point and the follow-up watcher. It fails without 19e3cc3;
  - a real-Docker snapshot-resume check, which is skipped when Docker is unavailable.
- **Rust:** `rust/tests/regression_176.rs` (17 tests) and `rust/tests/regression_176_recovery.rs` (15 tests) cover the same scenarios. The shell tests drive the real `start` binary through `--internal-recover-detached-docker`. Shared fixtures are in `rust/tests/support/issue_176.rs`.

Local checks:
- JS: `bun run check` passes; `bun run test` gives 1003 pass, 0 fail.
- Rust: `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` (no warnings) and `cargo test` (906 passed, 0 failed) all pass.
- Repo scripts: `node scripts/check-file-size.mjs` and `node scripts/check-test-parity.mjs` pass.

Also in this PR: the Security workflow's `npm-audit` job started failing on every branch because of new high-severity `brace-expansion` advisories (GHSA-q2hr-2g5m-vwhr, GHSA-qhr7-859c-m2p7, GHSA-6j4f-fj2g-mc7p). It is a dev dependency, pulled in through eslint > minimatch. The `package.json` override was raised to `^5.0.12`, and both lock files were updated, following 375bc56.

## Limitations

- Recovery needs execution tracking and a detached session whose only isolation level is `docker`. Nothing is recovered if the container has been removed.
- A `docker stop`/`docker kill` issued outside `$` looks like a kill (exit 137) and is recovered. Use `$ --stop <id>` to stop for good.
- A snapshot resume (`--resume <id> -- <cmd>`) or a relaunch of a removed session carries the resource limits, but not the recovery options. The new container has no selector.
- The marker stays in the container, so a later plain `--resume <id>` (`docker start`) runs the recovery command, not the original one.
- The `[Isolation] On kill ...` / `Resource limits` lines appear in the log and in `--status`, not in the terminal timeline. The timeline renderer only shows a fixed set of isolation fields, which predates this PR.

Release: `js/.changeset/issue-176.md` and `rust/changelog.d/176.md` (minor). README (Execution Tracking, Isolation Options), docs/USAGE.md and ARCHITECTURE.md (Detached Docker Completion) are updated.

issue.title: Docker `--resume <id> -- <cmd>` drops container resource limits, and there is no launch-time recovery command (one UUID / one log across OOM recovery)
issue.body:
## Summary

Two related gaps showed up in a real incident ([link-assistant/hive-mind#2408](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2408)). In that incident a long-running `$ --isolated docker --detached` AI work session was killed by the out-of-memory killer, and the supervisor needed to recover it:

1. **`$ --resume <id> -- <cmd>` drops the container's resource limits.** The `DOCKER_SNAPSHOT` plan in `src/lib/execution-resume.js` does `docker commit <old>` and then `docker run -d --name <session>-resume-N ...buildDockerRuntimeArgs(opts) <snapshot> sh -c <cmd>`. `buildDockerRuntimeArgs` only re-emits `--privileged`, `-e`, `-v`, `--mount`, `--network` and `--network-alias` (0.34.1, `src/lib/isolation.js:516`). Memory, swap, CPU and PIDs limits are not carried over: they were applied with `docker update`, or by an external start gate, and are not in the stored launch options. `docker commit` only captures the filesystem and image config, not the HostConfig. So the resumed container runs **without** the limits the original one had. A resumed session that just died of OOM is exactly the one most likely to blow up the host next.
2. **There is no way to declare a recovery command at launch time.** A supervisor that wants "run `A`; if the container is killed (OOM / SIGKILL), continue with `B` in the same filesystem" has to watch the session itself and issue `$ --resume <id> -- B` after the fact. If it can't (for example because of gap 1), it falls back to a fresh launch, and the work is then split across two execution UUIDs and two log files.

## Reproduction (gap 1)

```bash
# 1. Launch a detached docker session, then limit it the way a supervisor does
$ --isolated docker --detached --session demo -- sh -c 'sleep 600'
docker update --memory 256m --memory-swap 256m --cpus 0.5 demo
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' demo   # 268435456 500000000

# 2. Stop it and resume with a replacement command (DOCKER_SNAPSHOT path)
docker stop demo
$ --resume <execution-uuid> -- sh -c 'sleep 600'

# 3. The resumed container has no limits
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' demo-resume-1   # 0 0
```

Expected: the resumed container keeps the same Memory / MemorySwap / NanoCpus / CpuQuota / CpuPeriod / CpusetCpus / PidsLimit (and StorageOpt where the driver supports it) as the container it was snapshotted from.

## Workaround used in hive-mind

Hive-mind skips the in-place `$ --resume -- <cmd>` path whenever it applied resource limits (`planSameContainerResume` → `container-resource-limits`). Instead it launches a fresh session through its own start gate, which re-applies the limits. The new execution then lists the earlier execution UUIDs (`🆔 Execution: \`88951cec\` (earlier logs: \`0760afb4\`)`), so the full log can still be found ([link-assistant/hive-mind#2409](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2409)). The cost: a second UUID, a second log file, and a re-clone instead of continuing in the same working directory.

## Suggested fix

1. **Keep limits on snapshot resume.** Before `docker commit`, read `docker inspect <old>` and translate the non-zero HostConfig limits into `docker run` flags for the replacement container:

2. **Allow a recovery command at launch time**, for example:

   ```bash
       --on-kill-resume 3 --recovery-command 'solve … --resume-session' \
       -- solve …
   ```

## Environment

- start-command 0.34.1 (`$` from `bun add -g start-command`)
- Docker isolation, detached mode, Linux 6.8
