issue.title: Docker resume: re-apply resource limits on snapshot resume, add --on-kill-resume / --recovery-command (#176)
issue.body:
Fixes #176

## Problem

**1. `--resume <id> -- <cmd>` dropped the container's resource limits.** The snapshot resume (`DOCKER_SNAPSHOT`) runs `docker commit` and then `docker run` of a `<name>-resume-N` container. `docker commit` captures the filesystem and image config, but not HostConfig. So memory, CPU and PIDs limits did not carry over to the new container. This includes limits a supervisor applied with `docker update`, which were never in the stored launch options. Reproduced with `experiments/issue-176-docker-commit-drops-limits.sh`:

```
original: Memory=268435456 MemorySwap=268435456 NanoCpus=500000000 PidsLimit=64
resumed:  Memory=0 MemorySwap=0 NanoCpus=0 PidsLimit=<no value>
```

**2. There was no launch-time recovery.** When a detached container's main process was OOM-killed, the only way to continue was a new `$ --resume <id> -- <cmd>`. That needs an outside supervisor and starts a new container (losing problem 1's limits). There was no way to say at launch "on a kill, run this recovery command in the same container, under the same UUID and log".

## Fix (JS and Rust, same design)

### Resource limits survive a snapshot resume

- `docker-resource-limits.js` / `docker_resource_limits.rs` read the stopped container's limits with `docker inspect --format '{{json .HostConfig}}'` before the commit. They translate the non-default ones into `docker run` flags, only in combinations `docker run` accepts:
  - `--memory`, `--memory-swap` (only alongside `--memory`; `-1` is kept), `--memory-reservation`;
  - `--cpus`, or `--cpu-quota`/`--cpu-period` when `NanoCpus` is unset;
  - `--cpu-shares`, `--cpuset-cpus`, `--cpuset-mems`;
  - `--pids-limit`;
  - `--shm-size` (only when it differs from the 64m default), `--storage-opt`, `--ulimit`.
- The flags go into `docker run` for `-resume-N`. They are printed as an `[Isolation] Resource limits: ...` line, written to the log, stored as `resourceLimits` in the execution record, and included in the resume result (links notation, JSON and text). A later relaunch of a removed session re-applies the stored `resourceLimits` too.

### `--on-kill-resume <N>` / `--recovery-command <cmd>`

```bash
$ --isolated docker --detached --on-kill-resume 2 \
    --recovery-command 'agent --resume-from-checkpoint' -- agent --task build
```

- **Options.** Valid only with `--isolated docker` (as the only isolation level) and `--detached`. `--recovery-command` on its own implies one attempt. Both are stored in the record and listed in `--help`.
- **In the container.** The command is wrapped in a small `sh -c` selector. It runs the original argv unless the marker `/.start-command-recovery` exists. If it does, it runs the recovery command with `START_COMMAND_RECOVERY_ATTEMPT=<k>` exported.
- **In the completion watcher.** When the container exits with 137 or `OOMKilled=true`, a new branch runs before cleanup, footer and finalization. It hands off to the recovery step: `execution-recovery.js` in JS, `start --internal-recover-detached-docker` in Rust. The recovery step:
  - writes the post-mortem and a `[Recovery k/N]` separator into the **same log**;
  - logs the live `docker update` limits;
  - `docker cp`s the marker in and `docker start`s the **same container**, so the filesystem and HostConfig are unchanged;
  - records `recoveryAttempts`, `recoveryHistory` and `lastRecoveryAt` under the **same UUID**;
  - starts a new watcher that follows `docker logs -f --since <restart>`.

  When the attempts are used up, the watcher finalizes the run as before, with the real exit code.
- **`--stop`.** For such sessions `--stop` sets `stopRequestedAt` (and restores it if the stop fails), so a deliberate stop is never "recovered". A later `--resume` clears it.

## Reproducing

`experiments/issue-176-rust-e2e.sh [start-binary]` runs against real Docker. It launches with `--on-kill-resume 2`, applies `docker update --pids-limit 64`, then `docker kill`s the container three times. After that it applies `--memory 256m --memory-swap 256m --cpus 0.5` to the stopped container and runs a snapshot resume. Output with the Rust binary and, after the fix below, with the JS CLI:

```
running=true pids=64        # after kill 1: the same container is running again, limit intact
running=true                # after kill 2
running=false               # after kill 3: attempts used up
  exitCode 137
    resourceLimits --pids-limit=64
    recoveryAttempts 2
recovered attempt 1
recovered attempt 2
[Recovery] Not resuming: all 2 recovery attempt(s) used.
resume-1 mem=268435456 swap=268435456 cpus=500000000 pids=64
```

The real-Docker run also found a JS-only bug, fixed in 19e3cc3:
- `execution-recovery.js` ran its `main()` before `module.exports` was assigned. Its `require.main === module` block came first, and `docker-cleanup.js` requires the module back to build the next watcher.
- As a result, the container was restarted, but no watcher followed it, and the old watcher finalized the run as 137.

`experiments/issue-176-js-recovery-trace.sh` is the trace used to find it.

The host used here cannot *start* any container with a memory limit (`docker run --memory 256m alpine true` fails: `cannot enter cgroupv2 "/sys/fs/cgroup/docker" with domain controllers -- it is in threaded mode`). On this host, then, the memory/CPU part is verified on the resumed container's HostConfig (the last line above) rather than on a running process. PIDs limits are verified in both modes.

## Tests

- **JS:** `js/test/regression-176.js` has 34 tests:
  - HostConfig → flags parsing (defaults, swap rules, CPU exclusivity, shm, ulimits, storage-opt);
  - snapshot resume plans with and without `docker inspect`;
  - option parsing and validation;
  - the selector, run through a real `sh` with and without the marker;
  - recovery outcomes (resumed, attempts exhausted, stop requested, `docker cp`/`docker start` failures);
  - `--stop` marking;
  - the watcher run as a real shell against a stateful fake `docker`. This includes a new test that goes through the real `execution-recovery.js` entry point and the follow-up watcher. It fails without 19e3cc3;
  - a real-Docker snapshot-resume check, which is skipped when Docker is unavailable.
- **Rust:** `rust/tests/regression_176.rs` (17 tests) and `rust/tests/regression_176_recovery.rs` (15 tests) cover the same scenarios. The shell tests drive the real `start` binary through `--internal-recover-detached-docker`. Shared fixtures are in `rust/tests/support/issue_176.rs`.

Local checks:
- JS: `bun run check` passes; `bun run test` gives 1003 pass, 0 fail.
- Rust: `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` (no warnings) and `cargo test` (906 passed, 0 failed) all pass.
- Repo scripts: `node scripts/check-file-size.mjs` and `node scripts/check-test-parity.mjs` pass.

Also in this PR: the Security workflow's `npm-audit` job started failing on every branch because of new high-severity `brace-expansion` advisories (GHSA-q2hr-2g5m-vwhr, GHSA-qhr7-859c-m2p7, GHSA-6j4f-fj2g-mc7p). It is a dev dependency, pulled in through eslint > minimatch. The `package.json` override was raised to `^5.0.12`, and both lock files were updated, following 375bc56.

## Limitations

- Recovery needs execution tracking and a detached session whose only isolation level is `docker`. Nothing is recovered if the container has been removed.
- A `docker stop`/`docker kill` issued outside `$` looks like a kill (exit 137) and is recovered. Use `$ --stop <id>` to stop for good.
- A snapshot resume (`--resume <id> -- <cmd>`) or a relaunch of a removed session carries the resource limits, but not the recovery options. The new container has no selector.
- The marker stays in the container, so a later plain `--resume <id>` (`docker start`) runs the recovery command, not the original one.
- The `[Isolation] On kill ...` / `Resource limits` lines appear in the log and in `--status`, not in the terminal timeline. The timeline renderer only shows a fixed set of isolation fields, which predates this PR.

Release: `js/.changeset/issue-176.md` and `rust/changelog.d/176.md` (minor). README (Execution Tracking, Isolation Options), docs/USAGE.md and ARCHITECTURE.md (Detached Docker Completion) are updated.

issue.title: Docker `--resume <id> -- <cmd>` drops container resource limits, and there is no launch-time recovery command (one UUID / one log across OOM recovery)
issue.body:
## Summary

Two related gaps showed up in a real incident ([link-assistant/hive-mind#2408](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2408)). In that incident a long-running `$ --isolated docker --detached` AI work session was killed by the out-of-memory killer, and the supervisor needed to recover it:

1. **`$ --resume <id> -- <cmd>` drops the container's resource limits.** The `DOCKER_SNAPSHOT` plan in `src/lib/execution-resume.js` does `docker commit <old>` and then `docker run -d --name <session>-resume-N ...buildDockerRuntimeArgs(opts) <snapshot> sh -c <cmd>`. `buildDockerRuntimeArgs` only re-emits `--privileged`, `-e`, `-v`, `--mount`, `--network` and `--network-alias` (0.34.1, `src/lib/isolation.js:516`). Memory, swap, CPU and PIDs limits are not carried over: they were applied with `docker update`, or by an external start gate, and are not in the stored launch options. `docker commit` only captures the filesystem and image config, not the HostConfig. So the resumed container runs **without** the limits the original one had. A resumed session that just died of OOM is exactly the one most likely to blow up the host next.
2. **There is no way to declare a recovery command at launch time.** A supervisor that wants "run `A`; if the container is killed (OOM / SIGKILL), continue with `B` in the same filesystem" has to watch the session itself and issue `$ --resume <id> -- B` after the fact. If it can't (for example because of gap 1), it falls back to a fresh launch, and the work is then split across two execution UUIDs and two log files.

## Reproduction (gap 1)

```bash
# 1. Launch a detached docker session, then limit it the way a supervisor does
$ --isolated docker --detached --session demo -- sh -c 'sleep 600'
docker update --memory 256m --memory-swap 256m --cpus 0.5 demo
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' demo   # 268435456 500000000

# 2. Stop it and resume with a replacement command (DOCKER_SNAPSHOT path)
docker stop demo
$ --resume <execution-uuid> -- sh -c 'sleep 600'

# 3. The resumed container has no limits
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' demo-resume-1   # 0 0
```

Expected: the resumed container keeps the same Memory / MemorySwap / NanoCpus / CpuQuota / CpuPeriod / CpusetCpus / PidsLimit (and StorageOpt where the driver supports it) as the container it was snapshotted from.

## Workaround used in hive-mind

Hive-mind skips the in-place `$ --resume -- <cmd>` path whenever it applied resource limits (`planSameContainerResume` → `container-resource-limits`). Instead it launches a fresh session through its own start gate, which re-applies the limits. The new execution then lists the earlier execution UUIDs (`🆔 Execution: \`88951cec\` (earlier logs: \`0760afb4\`)`), so the full log can still be found ([link-assistant/hive-mind#2409](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2409)). The cost: a second UUID, a second log file, and a re-clone instead of continuing in the same working directory.

## Suggested fix

1. **Keep limits on snapshot resume.** Before `docker commit`, read `docker inspect <old>` and translate the non-zero HostConfig limits into `docker run` flags for the replacement container:
   `Memory → --memory`, `MemorySwap → --memory-swap`, `NanoCpus → --cpus`, `CpuQuota/CpuPeriod → --cpu-quota/--cpu-period`, `CpusetCpus → --cpuset-cpus`, `PidsLimit → --pids-limit`, `StorageOpt.size → --storage-opt size=…`, `ShmSize → --shm-size`, `Ulimits → --ulimit`. Print them in the `[Isolation]` status lines, and add a test that checks `docker inspect` of the `-resume-N` container. Optionally store the limits in the execution record, so a resume works even after the old container was removed.
2. **Allow a recovery command at launch time**, for example:
   ```bash
   $ --isolated docker --detached --session work \
       --on-kill-resume 3 --recovery-command 'solve … --resume-session' \
       -- solve …
   ```
   When the main process is killed by a signal (exit 137 / `OOMKilled`), start-command itself would run the recovery command in the same container. It would use `docker start` if the container still exists, or the snapshot path with the limits kept (fix 1) if not. It would keep the **same execution UUID**, append to the **same log file** with a clear `[Recovery 1/3] …` separator, and record the attempt count in `$ --status`. That gives supervisors one UUID and one log for the whole piece of work, which is what users asked for in hive-mind#2408 ("full log should be preserved under the same ID").

## Environment

- start-command 0.34.1 (`$` from `bun add -g start-command`)
- Docker isolation, detached mode, Linux 6.8

Found during [link-assistant/hive-mind#2408](https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2408).

issue.title: Detached docker watcher `docker rm -f`s a still-running container when `docker logs -f` fails (ENOSPC) and finalizes it as executed / exit 0
issue.body:
## Summary

With `$ --isolation docker --detached` and a log file, the completion watcher built by `buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript()` (`src/lib/docker-cleanup.js`, start-command **0.34.0**) assumes that `docker logs -f C >> LOG` only returns once the container has exited. It also returns when **its own write fails** — e.g. `ENOSPC` because the container filled the same disk the log is on — or when dockerd restarts (live-restore keeps the container running but drops follow streams).

The watcher then runs `docker inspect` on a container that is **still running**, which reports Docker's zero values `ExitCode=0 OOMKilled=false FinishedAt=0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`. As a result, it:

1. `docker rm -f`s the live container. This is what kills the workload.
2. Writes an `Exit Code: 0` footer.
3. Finalizes the execution record as `status: executed`, `exitCode: 0`. The only hint left is `endTimeSource: "observed-at"`.

Downstream this produced "✅ Work session finished successfully" for a 13.6-hour session that was actually killed when its 122.7 GB writable layer filled a 192.7 GB host disk: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2303 (case study: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2304).

## Reproducible example

`/dev/full` stands in for a full disk: every write to it fails with `ENOSPC`. Requires docker and `alpine:3.20`.

Script: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/blob/issue-2303-928b0c381ae1/experiments/issue-2303-watcher-enospc.mjs

Condensed:

```js
const { buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript, DOCKER_CONTAINER_CLEANUP_POLICY } = require('start-command/src/lib/docker-cleanup.js');
// docker run -d --name C alpine:3.20 sh -c 'while true; do echo work; sleep 0.1; done'
const script = buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript('C', DOCKER_CONTAINER_CLEANUP_POLICY.DEFAULT, '/dev/full', record.uuid);
spawnSync('sh', ['-c', script]);
```

Output with 0.34.0:

```
started container issue-2303-61821; running=true
state of a RUNNING container: 0 false 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z
watcher finished after 1826 ms (the container was never asked to stop)
sh: 1: printf: printf: I/O error
watcher saw exit=0 oom=false
container after watcher: REMOVED (docker rm -f killed the live session)
execution record after watcher: status=executed exitCode=0 exitReason=null
$ --status: { "status": "executed", "exitCode": 0, "endTimeSource": "observed-at", "oomKilled": false, ... }
```

Expected: the container keeps running, and the record stays `executing` until the container really exits (with its real exit code). At the very least, the watcher must not remove the container or report exit 0.

## Workarounds

- Put the start-command log folder on a different filesystem than Docker's data root (`/var/lib/docker`).
- Use `--keep-container`, so the watcher never removes the container. The record is still finalized too early.
- Consumers can treat `exitCode: 0` together with `endTimeSource: "observed-at"` for docker isolation as "not observed" (this is what hive-mind now does).

## Suggested fix

In `buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript()`:

```sh
docker logs -f C >> LOG 2>&1
# docker logs can return early (ENOSPC on LOG, daemon restart, signal): wait for the real exit
if [ "$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Running}}' C 2>/dev/null)" = true ]; then
  docker wait C >/dev/null 2>&1   # returns the real exit status once the container stops
fi
state=$(docker inspect ...)
```

- Treat a zero `FinishedAt` (`0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`) as "not finished", never as exit 0. Don't finalize the record in that state; use e.g. `exitReason: 'watcher-lost-container'` or leave it `executing`.
- Never `docker rm -f` a container whose `.State.Running` is `true`.
- The no-log branch already uses `docker wait` and is correct.

## Same class of bug: `code || 0`

A child killed by a signal has `code === null`. These places turn that into a successful exit 0:

- `src/lib/spawn-helpers.js:286`: `const exitCode = code || 0;`
- `src/lib/isolation-log-utils.js:197` (`runAsIsolatedUser`): `exitCode: code || 0`
- `src/lib/command-stream.js:57` and `:94`: `code: result.code || 0`

Suggested: `code ?? (signal ? 128 + os.constants.signals[signal] : 1)`, and record the signal.

issue.title: Detached docker watcher: wait for the real exit, never rm -f or finalize a running container as exit 0 (#174)
issue.body:
Fixes #174

## Problem

The detached Docker completion watcher treated the return of `docker logs -f C >> LOG` (or `docker wait C`) as proof that the container had exited. The command also returns in two other cases:

- its own write to LOG fails (ENOSPC, because the container filled the disk the log lives on);
- dockerd restarts under live-restore.

When that happened, the watcher inspected a **running** container. Docker's zero values are `ExitCode=0` and `FinishedAt=0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`. The watcher then:

- ran `docker rm -f` on the live workload,
- wrote an `Exit Code: 0` footer,
- finalized the record as `executed` / `0`.

## Fix (JS and Rust, same design)

- **Wait for the real exit.** After `docker logs -f` / `docker wait` returns, the watcher loops on `docker inspect -f '{{.State.Running}}'`, calling `docker wait` each time. `sleep 1` keeps a failing `docker wait` from spinning. If log capture stopped early, a note is written into the log.
- **Never touch a running container.** The state snippet records `.State.Running`. Cleanup (`docker rm -f`), the post-mortem, the `Exit Code:` footer and finalization now all sit behind `if [ "$__start_command_running" = true ]`.
  - If the container is still running, the watcher only appends `Container still running: <name>` with a hint, and the record stays `executing`.
  - The finalizer also refuses a running container (`reason: still-running`).
- **A zero `FinishedAt` is never exit 0.** `ExitCode=0` next to docker's zero `FinishedAt` becomes `-1` in both the shell and the finalizer. The record gets `exitReason: watcher-lost-container` and `endTimeSource: observed-at`. A real exit 0 with a real `FinishedAt` is still recorded as 0.
- **A signal death is never exit 0 (JS).** The new `resolveChildExitCode(code, signal)` returns `code` if it is numeric, otherwise `128 + os.constants.signals[signal]`, otherwise `1`. It replaces the `code || 0` sites the issue lists:
  - `spawn-helpers.js`
  - `isolation-log-utils.js` (which now also returns `signal`)
  - `command-stream.js` (both sites)
  - `cli.js`

  The Rust exit-code sites already fall back to `-1`/`1`, never `0`, so they are unchanged.

## Reproducing

`experiments/issue-174-watcher-enospc.mjs` needs real Docker and `alpine:3.20`. It runs a container that prints for about 3 s and then exits 7, and the watcher logs to `/dev/full`, so `docker logs -f` fails with ENOSPC immediately.

Before (0.34.0):
```
container after watcher: REMOVED
container state after watcher: REMOVED
record: status=executed exitCode=0 endTimeSource=observed-at
```

After:
```
watcher finished after 4549 ms
container after watcher: false
container state after watcher: 7 2026-09-27T16:57:03.546646518Z
record: status=executed exitCode=7 endTimeSource=docker-finished-at exitReason=undefined
```

## Tests

- `js/test/regression-174.js` (14 tests) runs the real generated watcher against a stateful fake `docker`. The fake scripts successive `.State.Running` answers, including a failing inspect as during a dockerd restart, and records whether each `rm` happened while the container was running. The file covers:
  - waiting after ENOSPC;
  - `rm` only after the exit;
  - a daemon restart;
  - the no-log branch;
  - never removing, footering or finalizing a running container;
  - a zero `FinishedAt` giving `-1` / `watcher-lost-container`;
  - the finalizer's refusal while running;
  - a real exit 0 still being recorded;
  - `resolveChildExitCode`;
  - a `kill -KILL $$` child giving `137` through `runWithNodeSpawn`.

  13 of the 14 fail on the old code.
- `rust/tests/regression_174.rs` (10 tests) covers the same scenarios. The generated watcher calls the real `start` binary for finalization. With the watcher change reverted, all 7 shell tests fail.
- `regression_170` (JS and Rust): the "no finish time" test used to assert `exitCode 0` for `ExitCode=0` plus a zero `FinishedAt`, which is exactly the #174 bug. It now expects `-1` / `watcher-lost-container`.

Local checks:
- JS: `bun run check` passes; `bun run test` gives 969 pass, 0 fail.
- Rust: `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` (no warnings) and `cargo test` all pass.

Release: `js/.changeset/issue-174.md` (patch) and `rust/changelog.d/174.md` (patch). README and ARCHITECTURE now describe the wait.

issue.title: Detached docker watcher: wait for the real exit, never rm -f or finalize a running container as exit 0 (#174)
issue.body:
Fixes #174

## Problem

The detached Docker completion watcher treated the return of `docker logs -f C >> LOG` (or `docker wait C`) as proof that the container had exited. The command also returns in two other cases:

- its own write to LOG fails (ENOSPC, because the container filled the disk the log lives on);
- dockerd restarts under live-restore.

When that happened, the watcher inspected a **running** container. Docker's zero values are `ExitCode=0` and `FinishedAt=0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`. The watcher then:

- ran `docker rm -f` on the live workload,
- wrote an `Exit Code: 0` footer,
- finalized the record as `executed` / `0`.

## Fix (JS and Rust, same design)

- **Wait for the real exit.** After `docker logs -f` / `docker wait` returns, the watcher loops on `docker inspect -f '{{.State.Running}}'`, calling `docker wait` each time. `sleep 1` keeps a failing `docker wait` from spinning. If log capture stopped early, a note is written into the log.
- **Never touch a running container.** The state snippet records `.State.Running`. Cleanup (`docker rm -f`), the post-mortem, the `Exit Code:` footer and finalization now all sit behind `if [ "$__start_command_running" = true ]`.
  - If the container is still running, the watcher only appends `Container still running: <name>` with a hint, and the record stays `executing`.
  - The finalizer also refuses a running container (`reason: still-running`).
- **A zero `FinishedAt` is never exit 0.** `ExitCode=0` next to docker's zero `FinishedAt` becomes `-1` in both the shell and the finalizer. The record gets `exitReason: watcher-lost-container` and `endTimeSource: observed-at`. A real exit 0 with a real `FinishedAt` is still recorded as 0.
- **A signal death is never exit 0 (JS).** The new `resolveChildExitCode(code, signal)` returns `code` if it is numeric, otherwise `128 + os.constants.signals[signal]`, otherwise `1`. It replaces the `code || 0` sites the issue lists:
  - `spawn-helpers.js`
  - `isolation-log-utils.js` (which now also returns `signal`)
  - `command-stream.js` (both sites)
  - `cli.js`

  The Rust exit-code sites already fall back to `-1`/`1`, never `0`, so they are unchanged.

## Reproducing

`experiments/issue-174-watcher-enospc.mjs` needs real Docker and `alpine:3.20`. It runs a container that prints for about 3 s and then exits 7, and the watcher logs to `/dev/full`, so `docker logs -f` fails with ENOSPC immediately.

watcher finished after 4549 ms
container after watcher: false
container state after watcher: 7 2026-09-27T16:57:03.546646518Z
record: status=executed exitCode=7 endTimeSource=docker-finished-at exitReason=undefined
```

## Tests

- `js/test/regression-174.js` (14 tests) runs the real generated watcher against a stateful fake `docker`. The fake scripts successive `.State.Running` answers, including a failing inspect as during a dockerd restart, and records whether each `rm` happened while the container was running. The file covers:
  - waiting after ENOSPC;
  - `rm` only after the exit;
  - a daemon restart;
  - the no-log branch;
  - never removing, footering or finalizing a running container;
  - a zero `FinishedAt` giving `-1` / `watcher-lost-container`;
  - the finalizer's refusal while running;
  - a real exit 0 still being recorded;
  - `resolveChildExitCode`;
  - a `kill -KILL $$` child giving `137` through `runWithNodeSpawn`.

  13 of the 14 fail on the old code.
- `rust/tests/regression_174.rs` (10 tests) covers the same scenarios. The generated watcher calls the real `start` binary for finalization. With the watcher change reverted, all 7 shell tests fail.

issue.title: Detached docker watcher `docker rm -f`s a still-running container when `docker logs -f` fails (ENOSPC) and finalizes it as executed / exit 0
issue.body:
## Summary

With `$ --isolation docker --detached` and a log file, the completion watcher built by `buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript()` (`src/lib/docker-cleanup.js`, start-command **0.34.0**) assumes that `docker logs -f C >> LOG` only returns once the container has exited. It also returns when **its own write fails** — e.g. `ENOSPC` because the container filled the same disk the log is on — or when dockerd restarts (live-restore keeps the container running but drops follow streams).

The watcher then runs `docker inspect` on a container that is **still running**, which reports Docker's zero values `ExitCode=0 OOMKilled=false FinishedAt=0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`. As a result, it:

1. `docker rm -f`s the live container. This is what kills the workload.
2. Writes an `Exit Code: 0` footer.
3. Finalizes the execution record as `status: executed`, `exitCode: 0`. The only hint left is `endTimeSource: "observed-at"`.

Downstream this produced "✅ Work session finished successfully" for a 13.6-hour session that was actually killed when its 122.7 GB writable layer filled a 192.7 GB host disk: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2303 (case study: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2304).

## Reproducible example

`/dev/full` stands in for a full disk: every write to it fails with `ENOSPC`. Requires docker and `alpine:3.20`.

Script: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/blob/issue-2303-928b0c381ae1/experiments/issue-2303-watcher-enospc.mjs

Condensed:

```js
const { buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript, DOCKER_CONTAINER_CLEANUP_POLICY } = require('start-command/src/lib/docker-cleanup.js');
// docker run -d --name C alpine:3.20 sh -c 'while true; do echo work; sleep 0.1; done'
const script = buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript('C', DOCKER_CONTAINER_CLEANUP_POLICY.DEFAULT, '/dev/full', record.uuid);
spawnSync('sh', ['-c', script]);
```

Output with 0.34.0:

```
started container issue-2303-61821; running=true
state of a RUNNING container: 0 false 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z
watcher finished after 1826 ms (the container was never asked to stop)
sh: 1: printf: printf: I/O error
watcher saw exit=0 oom=false
container after watcher: REMOVED (docker rm -f killed the live session)
execution record after watcher: status=executed exitCode=0 exitReason=null
$ --status: { "status": "executed", "exitCode": 0, "endTimeSource": "observed-at", "oomKilled": false, ... }
```

Expected: the container keeps running, and the record stays `executing` until the container really exits (with its real exit code). At the very least, the watcher must not remove the container or report exit 0.

## Workarounds

- Put the start-command log folder on a different filesystem than Docker's data root (`/var/lib/docker`).
- Use `--keep-container`, so the watcher never removes the container. The record is still finalized too early.
- Consumers can treat `exitCode: 0` together with `endTimeSource: "observed-at"` for docker isolation as "not observed" (this is what hive-mind now does).

## Suggested fix

In `buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript()`:

```sh
docker logs -f C >> LOG 2>&1
# docker logs can return early (ENOSPC on LOG, daemon restart, signal): wait for the real exit
if [ "$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Running}}' C 2>/dev/null)" = true ]; then
  docker wait C >/dev/null 2>&1   # returns the real exit status once the container stops
fi
state=$(docker inspect ...)
```

- Treat a zero `FinishedAt` (`0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`) as "not finished", never as exit 0. Don't finalize the record in that state; use e.g. `exitReason: 'watcher-lost-container'` or leave it `executing`.
- Never `docker rm -f` a container whose `.State.Running` is `true`.
- The no-log branch already uses `docker wait` and is correct.

## Same class of bug: `code || 0`

A child killed by a signal has `code === null`. These places turn that into a successful exit 0:

- `src/lib/spawn-helpers.js:286`: `const exitCode = code || 0;`
- `src/lib/isolation-log-utils.js:197` (`runAsIsolatedUser`): `exitCode: code || 0`
- `src/lib/command-stream.js:57` and `:94`: `code: result.code || 0`

Suggested: `code ?? (signal ? 128 + os.constants.signals[signal] : 1)`, and record the signal.

issue.title: fix: persist detached docker terminal state and record the container post-mortem
issue.body:
## Summary

Repository-mode PR for #172: one pull request implementing both sub-issues, in
**both** implementations (JavaScript and Rust), plus the attached-Docker path
the sub-issues do not mention but which had the same defect.

Neither sub-issue was already resolved — both were reproduced with failing
tests before anything was fixed.

## #170 — the detached terminal state was never persisted

A detached Docker execution's completion watcher streamed the logs, decided on
cleanup, wrote the footer — and then left the store record `executing` forever.
`--status` papered over the gap by calling the clock at query time, so every
query invented a different "finish" time for the same finished command.

**170.1 — write the terminal state back into the store.**
The watcher now re-invokes the CLI once the container is gone and persists
`status`, the real `exitCode`, `oomKilled` and a real `endTime`. Bookkeeping
runs **last**, after the log footer, so a record only becomes terminal once its
log is complete — asserted by comparing string offsets in the generated script.

Dispatch differs by necessity: JavaScript re-invokes `detached-finalize.js`
through the runtime, Rust re-invokes its own binary via `current_exe()` with a
hidden `--internal-finalize-detached-docker` flag, handled before argument
parsing so it never appears in `--help`.

**170.2 — stop calling `new Date()` at query time.**
Precedence is `State.FinishedAt` → the log footer's `Finished:` line →
observation time, and the result is *marked*: `endTimeSource` is one of
`docker-finished-at`, `log-footer`, `observed-at`, and the last also sets
`observedAt`. The footer parser returns both facts (exit code *and* timestamp)
instead of the exit code alone.

Root cause found while wiring this up: the shell footer snippet used local
`date` while the in-process footer wrote UTC, so the two writers of the same
`Finished:` line disagreed on timezone. Both now use `date -u`.

**170.3 — `cleanupStale` must not fabricate a finish time.**
A lost execution now keeps `endTime` empty and records `staleDetectedAt`. The
moment cleanup noticed is not the moment the command stopped, and conflating
them is exactly the bug this issue is about.

**170.4 — signal deaths.**
Taken as the documented option: `status` answers one question — *is this still
running?* — and README now says so explicitly. The cause of death is carried by
`exitCode` (decoded: `137 (SIGKILL - 128+9)`), `oomKilled`, `exitReason` and the
post-mortem. Adding `killed`/`terminated` statuses would have made `status` a
verdict again, which #148/#151/#162/#165 deliberately moved away from.

## #171 — "Container kept for investigation" omitted the post-mortem

**171.1** The watcher's single `docker inspect` now collects
`{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.StartedAt}} {{.State.FinishedAt}}`
plus `{{.State.Error}}` (read separately — it is free-form text that can contain
spaces, so it cannot ride along in a whitespace-split template).

**171.2** A kept container's log ends with the facts, before the footer:

```
=== Container post-mortem ===
Container:  my-docker-session
Exit Code:  137 (SIGKILL - 128+9)
OOMKilled:  false
StartedAt:  2026-09-15T22:21:40.942007645Z
FinishedAt: 2026-09-15T22:21:46.740817278Z
Lifetime:   5.798s
Error:      (none)
```

**171.3** A removed container states the same facts in one line, written before
it stops existing:

```
Container removed: my-docker-session (exit 137, SIGKILL, lifetime 5.798s, oomKilled=false)
```

**171.4** Signal decoding is hoisted into a single `describeExitCode()` /
`describe_exit_code()`. It lives in `exit-reason.js` / `exit_reason.rs` rather
than the log-utils module the issue suggested, because `SIGNAL_NAMES` already
lives there and that module is dependency-free — putting it in log-utils created
an import cycle. Log-utils re-exports it, so both call sites the issue names are
satisfied. The watcher's shell `case` table is *generated from the same table*,
so the log and `--status` can never name different signals for the same code.

**171.5** `exitReason` is persisted alongside the record.

## Beyond the two sub-issues

The **attached** Docker path had the same gap: it inspected `State.OOMKilled`
alone, so its "Container kept for investigation" message could not say what
killed the container, and a removed one took its facts with it. It now reads the
same five fields in one inspect, before any `docker rm`, and reuses the same
formatters. `readDockerContainerOomKilled` / `read_docker_container_oom_killed`
are gone — the new reader returns that flag alongside the rest.

Docker's zero-time sentinel `0001-01-01T00:00:00Z` is rejected everywhere, so a
year-1 timestamp can never reach a record or a log.

## Dependencies

None added, after checking the alternatives: `dockerode` / `bollard` would
replace a tiny `sh -c` watcher that must *outlive* the CLI process, which is the
one thing a library bound to that process cannot do; `docker events` has the
same lifetime problem; and a ten-entry signal table does not justify a `signal` /
`nix` dependency.

## How to reproduce

```bash
$ --detached --docker -- sh -c 'sleep 1; exit 137'
$ --status <uuid>          # before: status executing, endTime = now, different on every call
$ --status <uuid>          # after:  status executed, exitCode 137 (SIGKILL - 128+9),
                           #         endTime fixed, endTimeSource docker-finished-at
cat <logPath>              # after:  === Container post-mortem === before the footer
```

## Tests

New, written before the fixes:

- `js/test/regression-170.js` — 10 tests
- `js/test/regression-171.js` — 22 tests (6 cover the attached path)
- `rust/tests/regression_170.rs` — 9 tests
- `rust/tests/regression_171.rs` — 12 tests, including `/bin/sh` execution of the
  generated snippets against a fake `docker` on `PATH`
- watcher-shape and attached-path unit tests in `docker-cleanup.js` /
  `docker_cleanup.rs` (the Rust generators are `pub(crate)`, so those assertions
  have to live in-file)
- `rust/tests/cleanup.rs` and `js/test/execution-store.js` updated for the new
  `staleDetectedAt` semantics

Local verification: JS `bun run check` clean, 953 pass / 0 fail across 53 files;
Rust `cargo fmt`/`cargo clippy --all-targets` clean, 862 pass / 0 fail; file-size
check and test parity (932 Rust / 902 JS = 103.3%) both pass.

## Note on file splits

Two files crossed the repository's 1000-line limit and were split along their
existing seams: `isolation.rs` → `isolation_shell.rs`, and `status_formatter.rs`
→ `status_footer.rs` (footer parsing) + `status_probe.rs` (live backend
probing). No behaviour moved with them.

Fixes #170
Fixes #171
Fixes #172

issue.title: Detached Docker: "Container kept for investigation" log omits the post-mortem facts (signal, StartedAt/FinishedAt, State) that are available at that exact moment
issue.body:
## Summary

When a detached Docker container exits non-zero, start-command deliberately keeps it "for investigation" and writes that decision into the session log:

```
Container kept for investigation: 04d07ec8-1e0e-4866-b7a3-cea8049552c3
Reason: exitCode=137 oomKilled=false
```

But the log — the **only artifact that outlives the container** — never records *what actually happened to the container*. It does not name the signal, it does not carry `StartedAt`/`FinishedAt`, and it does not carry the `State` snapshot. All of that is available to the completion watcher at the moment it writes those lines, and `exitReason "signal (SIGKILL)"` is even computed by `$ --status` — but only in memory, at query time, and only while the record can still be enriched.

The result is that "kept for investigation" preserves a container that the host will eventually reap, and a log that cannot answer the first question of the investigation: *was it killed, and by what?*

Reproduced on **start-command 0.33.0** (latest on npm), Node v26.3.0, Linux, Docker isolation.

## Reproduction

```bash
session="$(cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/uuid)"
$ --isolated docker --image alpine:3.20 --shell sh \
  --detached --session "$session" -- 'sleep 300' | tee /tmp/launch.log

log_path="$(grep -o '/tmp/start-command/logs/isolation/docker/[^ ]*\.log' /tmp/launch.log | head -n1)"

sleep 5
docker kill --signal KILL "$session"       # exit 137, not an OOM
sleep 3                                     # let the completion watcher finish

echo "--- what the log knows ---"
tail -n 12 "$log_path"
grep -ci 'signal\|sigkill' "$log_path"     # => 0

echo "--- what Docker knew at that moment ---"
docker inspect -f '{{.State.StartedAt}} {{.State.FinishedAt}} {{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' "$session"

echo "--- what --status can still compute, but never wrote down ---"
$ --status "$session" | grep -E 'exitReason|exitCode'
```

## Observed

Log tail (complete, nothing omitted):

```
Container kept for investigation: 04d07ec8-1e0e-4866-b7a3-cea8049552c3
Reason: exitCode=137 oomKilled=false
Re-enter while running: $ --attach 04d07ec8-1e0e-4866-b7a3-cea8049552c3
Continue the stored command: $ --resume 04d07ec8-1e0e-4866-b7a3-cea8049552c3
Run another command in the same container: $ --resume 04d07ec8-1e0e-4866-b7a3-cea8049552c3 -- <command>
Remove when done: docker rm -f 04d07ec8-1e0e-4866-b7a3-cea8049552c3

==================================================
Finished: 2026-09-15 22:21:47.014
Exit Code: 137
```

`grep -ci 'signal\|sigkill'` over the whole log → **0**.

Docker, at the same instant:

```
StartedAt  2026-09-15T22:21:40.942007645Z
FinishedAt 2026-09-15T22:21:46.740817278Z
ExitCode   137
OOMKilled  false
```

`$ --status`, at the same instant:

```
  exitCode 137
  exitReason "signal (SIGKILL)"
```

So `exitReason` exists, is correct, and is thrown away. Once the container is gone, `--status` can no longer produce it either — `readDockerState()` returns `null` and the enrichment branch that computes the reason never runs. The knowledge is lost permanently, even though it was in memory in the process that owned the log file.

## Why this matters in practice

`exitCode=137 oomKilled=false` is the single most ambiguous line a post-mortem can start from. It is consistent with at least: an external `docker kill`, a host OOM killer acting on the container's processes without setting the cgroup flag, a supervisor `kill -9`, and a nested-daemon kill. Distinguishing them needs exactly the facts that were available and not written: the signal, the container lifetime, and the `State` block.

In link-assistant/hive-mind#2244 this cost days: a task container died 5.6 s after start, and the surviving evidence was a 37-line log ending in `Reason: exitCode=137 oomKilled=false`. There was no way to tell whether the workload had ever begun.

## Suggested fix

Extend `buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript()` in `src/lib/docker-cleanup.js` (~line 234). It already runs:

```js
parts.push(
  `__start_command_state=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' ${quotedName} 2>/dev/null || printf '%s' '-1 false')`
);
```

**1. Fetch the whole picture in that one call** — it is free:

```js
`docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.StartedAt}} {{.State.FinishedAt}} {{.State.Error}}' ${quotedName}`
```

**2. Append a post-mortem block to the log** whenever the container is kept (i.e. inside the `else` branch of `buildDockerKeptLogSnippet()`), before the footer:

```
=== Container post-mortem ===
Exit Code:  137 (SIGKILL — 128+9)
OOMKilled:  false
StartedAt:  2026-09-15T22:21:40.942007645Z
FinishedAt: 2026-09-15T22:21:46.740817278Z
Lifetime:   5.8s
Error:
```

The signal decoding is the same mapping `exitReason` already uses (`128 + n` → signal name) — it just needs to move from `status-formatter.js` (query time, in-memory) into the watcher (completion time, on disk). Hoisting it into a shared helper, e.g. `describeExitCode(exitCode)` in `src/lib/isolation-log-utils.js`, lets both call sites share one implementation.

**3. Consider writing the same block on the removal path too.** When the policy removes the container, the loss is total: after `docker rm -f` nothing is inspectable, so a log line is the only possible record. Even a single line — `Container removed (exit 137, SIGKILL, lifetime 5.8s, oomKilled=false)` — closes the gap.

**4. Optionally persist `exitReason`** alongside the record (see #170, which covers the store side of the same gap).

## Workaround

Snapshot the container host-side before anything can remove it:

```bash
docker inspect "$session"          > "$log_path.diagnostics/container-inspect.json"
docker logs   "$session" > "$log_path.diagnostics/container-logs.txt" 2>&1
```

That is what we now do in the supervisor — a sidecar `<session>.log.diagnostics/` directory written at completion time, before reaping — precisely because the session log could not be relied on to carry these facts.

## Context

Found while investigating link-assistant/hive-mind#2244. Full case study and the host-side mitigation: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2245

Related: #170 (terminal state / `endTime` not persisted), #138 (session log omits the image-preparation phase) — all three are instances of "a fact was known at the time and not written into the one file that survives".

issue.title: Detached Docker: terminal state is never persisted, and `$ --status` fabricates `endTime` from `new Date()` at query time
issue.body:
## Summary For a **detached Docker** session, the terminal state of the run is never written back to the execution store. The record stays `status "executing"`, `exitCode null`, `endTime null` forever, even after the container has exited and start-command's own completion watcher has already appended `Exit Code: 137` to the session log. `$ --status` hides this by recomputing the state on every query — and while doing so it **fabricates `endTime` from `new Date()`**. The consequence is that `endTime` is not the time the command finished, it is the time you happened to ask. It moves on every query, and it can be arbitrarily far from reality: in the incident that led me here, `$ --status` reported an `endTime` roughly **four days** after the container's real `FinishedAt`, because that was simply when we ran the query. Reproduced on **start-command 0.33.0** (latest on npm at the time of writing), Node v26.3.0, Linux, Docker isolation. ## Reproduction Self-contained script (no dependencies beyond `docker`, `node` and `$`):
start-command-detached-terminal-state.sh ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # Minimal reproducer: a detached Docker session that is SIGKILLed never gets its # terminal state persisted, and `$ --status` fabricates `endTime` at query time. set -euo pipefail out="${1:-/tmp/start-command-detached-terminal-state}" session="$(cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/uuid)" mkdir -p "$out" trap 'docker rm -f "$session" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true' EXIT echo "[1/5] launching a detached docker session (session=$session)" \$ --isolated docker --image alpine:3.20 --shell sh \ --detached --session "$session" \ -- 'sleep 300' >"$out/launch.log" 2>&1 || true log_path="$(grep -o '/tmp/start-command/logs/isolation/docker/[^ ]*\.log' "$out/launch.log" | head -n1)" execution_id="$(basename "$log_path" .log)" echo "[2/5] SIGKILL after 5s (exit 137, not an OOM)" sleep 5 docker kill --signal KILL "$session" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true sleep 3 # let the detached completion watcher append its block docker inspect "$session" >"$out/inspect.json" 2>/dev/null || true cp "$log_path" "$out/session.log" echo "[3/5] first \$ --status" \$ --status "$session" >"$out/status-1.txt" 2>&1 || true echo "[4/5] reading the persisted record straight out of the store" node -e ' const fs = require("fs"); const text = fs.readFileSync(process.env.HOME + "/.start-command/executions.lino", "utf8"); const decoded = text.replace(/\(str ([A-Za-z0-9+/=]+)\)/g, (_, b64) => `"${Buffer.from(b64, "base64").toString("utf8")}"`); const at = decoded.indexOf(process.argv[1]); const slice = at === -1 ? "" : decoded.slice(at, at + 1200); for (const key of ["status", "exitCode", "endTime"]) { const m = slice.match(new RegExp(`"${key}"\\s+([^)]*)`)); console.log(`persisted ${key} = ${m ? m[1].trim() : ""}`); } ' "$execution_id" >"$out/stored-record.txt" 2>&1 || true echo "[5/5] second \$ --status, 4s later (a *persisted* endTime cannot move)" sleep 4 \$ --status "$session" >"$out/status-2.txt" 2>&1 || true { echo "container_started_at=$(node -p 'JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync(process.argv[1],"utf8"))[0].State.StartedAt' "$out/inspect.json")" echo "container_finished_at=$(node -p 'JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync(process.argv[1],"utf8"))[0].State.FinishedAt' "$out/inspect.json")" echo "status_endTime_query_1=$(grep -o 'endTime.*' "$out/status-1.txt" | head -n1)" echo "status_endTime_query_2=$(grep -o 'endTime.*' "$out/status-2.txt" | head -n1)" cat "$out/stored-record.txt" } | tee "$out/summary.txt" ```
## Observed output ``` container_started_at=2026-09-15T22:21:40.942007645Z container_finished_at=2026-09-15T22:21:46.740817278Z status_endTime_query_1=endTime "2026-09-15T22:21:50.337Z" status_endTime_query_2=endTime "2026-09-15T22:21:54.723Z" persisted status = "executing" persisted exitCode = (null persisted endTime = (null ``` Three distinct problems are visible in those six lines: 1. **Nothing terminal is persisted.** The container exited at `22:21:46.740`, `docker inspect` says `ExitCode: 137`, and the session log already ends with `Finished: 2026-09-15 22:21:47.014` / `Exit Code: 137` — yet the store still says `executing` / `null` / `null`. 2. **`endTime` is fabricated at query time.** Query 1 says `22:21:50.337Z`, query 4 seconds later says `22:21:54.723Z`. Neither is the finish time; both are "now". 3. **`endTime` drifts unboundedly.** Since it is always "now", querying a week later yields a timestamp a week after the real finish. That is exactly what bit us: a container that died on `2026-09-09 17:43:07` was reported with an `endTime` of `2026-09-13…`, which sent the investigation down the wrong path (we believed the task had run for days). Once the container is removed (`docker rm -f`), the `--status` output does become terminal (`status executed`) — but by then `exitCode` and `endTime` are derived from the log footer / the `-1` fallback, and `endTime` is still `new Date()`. ## Root cause in the code The detached completion watcher already has the authoritative facts — it inspects the container and reads `.State.ExitCode` and `.State.OOMKilled` — but it only uses them to decide whether to remove the container and what to print into the log. It never calls back into the execution store: `src/lib/docker-cleanup.js` (`buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript`, ~line 234): ```js parts.push(`docker logs -f ${quotedName} >> ${quotedLogPath} 2>&1`); parts.push( `__start_command_state=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' ${quotedName} 2>/dev/null || printf '%s' '-1 false')` ); parts.push('__start_command_exit=${__start_command_state%% *}'); parts.push('__start_command_oom=${__start_command_state##* }'); … parts.push(`${createShellLogFooterSnippet()} >> ${quotedLogPath}`); ``` `__start_command_exit` reaches the log and then is dropped on the floor. The record in `~/.start-command/executions.lino` is never updated, so every later reader has to re-derive the outcome. That re-derivation is `resolveDetachedStatus()` in `src/lib/status-formatter.js`, which fills the hole with wall-clock time in three places: ```js // line 271 if (!enriched.endTime) { enriched.endTime = new Date().toISOString(); } // line 285 (same, for the OOM branch) // line 327 (same, for the "not alive but record says executing" branch) ``` `src/lib/execution-store.js:668` does the same for stale records (`currentRecords[index].endTime = new Date().toISOString()`). `new Date()` is a correct default only when the record is being finalized *at the moment the process ends*. In the detached-Docker path it is being finalized whenever someone happens to run `--status`, which can be days later, so the value is not an approximation of the finish time — it is unrelated to it. ## Suggested fix **1. Persist the terminal state from the completion watcher.** The watcher is the one place that reliably observes the end of the run. After the `docker inspect` line in `buildDetachedDockerCompletionScript()`, add a step that writes the outcome back, e.g. by invoking the CLI's own store from the same shell script: ```js parts.push( `${shellQuote(process.execPath)} ${shellQuote(finalizeScriptPath)} ` + `${shellQuote(executionId)} "$__start_command_exit" "$__start_command_oom" ` + `"$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.FinishedAt}}' ${quotedName} 2>/dev/null)" ` + `>/dev/null 2>&1 || true` ); ``` where `finalize.js` loads `ExecutionStore`, sets `status = executed`, `exitCode`, `oomKilled` and `endTime` from the passed `FinishedAt`, and saves under the existing lock. `docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}'` is already being run there, so extending it to `'{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.StartedAt}} {{.State.FinishedAt}}'` costs nothing. **2. Stop inventing `endTime`.** In `resolveDetachedStatus()`, derive it, in order of preference, from: * `dockerState` — `.State.FinishedAt` (already fetched by `readDockerState()` for docker records; it is the ground truth); * the log footer, which already carries `Finished: 2026-09-15 22:21:47.014` next to the `Exit Code:` line the function parses anyway (`parseExitCodeFromTail` could return both); * only then fall back — and when falling back, mark it, e.g. `endTimeSource: "observed-at"` or leave `endTime` null and expose `observedAt` instead. A `null` endTime is honest; a wrong one silently corrupts every downstream duration calculation. The same applies to `execution-store.js:668`: a stale-record sweep genuinely does not know when the process died, so `endTime` there should be recorded as an observation (`staleDetectedAt`) rather than as the finish time. **3. (Minor, same area.)** `$ --status` reports `status executed` together with `exitCode 137` and `exitReason "signal (SIGKILL)"`. `executed` reading as "finished" is defensible, but a consumer that branches on `status` alone treats a SIGKILLed run as a completed one. Consider a distinct terminal status (`killed`/`terminated`) or documenting explicitly that `status` only means "no longer running". ## Workaround Do not trust `endTime` (or `status`) from `--status` for detached Docker sessions. Take the timestamps from Docker before the container is removed: ```bash docker inspect -f '{{.State.StartedAt}} {{.State.FinishedAt}} {{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' "$session" ``` and persist that snapshot host-side yourself. That is what we ended up doing — we now capture `docker inspect` + `docker logs` into a sidecar directory before reaping the container, because the session record could not be relied on. ## Context Found while investigating link-assistant/hive-mind#2244, where a Docker-isolated task was SIGKILLed 5.6 s into startup and the only surviving artifacts were a 37-line session log and a `$ --status` output whose `endTime` was days off. Full case study: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/pull/2245

issue.title: fix: persist detached docker terminal state and record the container post-mortem
issue.body:
## Summary

Repository-mode PR for #172: one pull request implementing both sub-issues, in
**both** implementations (JavaScript and Rust), plus the attached-Docker path
the sub-issues do not mention but which had the same defect.

Neither sub-issue was already resolved — both were reproduced with failing
tests before anything was fixed.

## #170 — the detached terminal state was never persisted

A detached Docker execution's completion watcher streamed the logs, decided on
cleanup, wrote the footer — and then left the store record `executing` forever.
`--status` papered over the gap by calling the clock at query time, so every
query invented a different "finish" time for the same finished command.

**170.1 — write the terminal state back into the store.**
The watcher now re-invokes the CLI once the container is gone and persists
`status`, the real `exitCode`, `oomKilled` and a real `endTime`. Bookkeeping
runs **last**, after the log footer, so a record only becomes terminal once its
log is complete — asserted by comparing string offsets in the generated script.

Dispatch differs by necessity: JavaScript re-invokes `detached-finalize.js`
through the runtime, Rust re-invokes its own binary via `current_exe()` with a
hidden `--internal-finalize-detached-docker` flag, handled before argument
parsing so it never appears in `--help`.

**170.2 — stop calling `new Date()` at query time.**
Precedence is `State.FinishedAt` → the log footer's `Finished:` line →
observation time, and the result is *marked*: `endTimeSource` is one of
`docker-finished-at`, `log-footer`, `observed-at`, and the last also sets
`observedAt`. The footer parser returns both facts (exit code *and* timestamp)
instead of the exit code alone.

Root cause found while wiring this up: the shell footer snippet used local
`date` while the in-process footer wrote UTC, so the two writers of the same
`Finished:` line disagreed on timezone. Both now use `date -u`.

**170.3 — `cleanupStale` must not fabricate a finish time.**
A lost execution now keeps `endTime` empty and records `staleDetectedAt`. The
moment cleanup noticed is not the moment the command stopped, and conflating
them is exactly the bug this issue is about.

**170.4 — signal deaths.**
Taken as the documented option: `status` answers one question — *is this still
running?* — and README now says so explicitly. The cause of death is carried by
`exitCode` (decoded: `137 (SIGKILL - 128+9)`), `oomKilled`, `exitReason` and the
post-mortem. Adding `killed`/`terminated` statuses would have made `status` a
verdict again, which #148/#151/#162/#165 deliberately moved away from.

## #171 — "Container kept for investigation" omitted the post-mortem

**171.1** The watcher's single `docker inspect` now collects
`{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.StartedAt}} {{.State.FinishedAt}}`
plus `{{.State.Error}}` (read separately — it is free-form text that can contain
spaces, so it cannot ride along in a whitespace-split template).

**171.2** A kept container's log ends with the facts, before the footer:

```
=== Container post-mortem ===
Container:  my-docker-session
Exit Code:  137 (SIGKILL - 128+9)
OOMKilled:  false
StartedAt:  2026-09-15T22:21:40.942007645Z
FinishedAt: 2026-09-15T22:21:46.740817278Z
Lifetime:   5.798s
Error:      (none)
```

**171.3** A removed container states the same facts in one line, written before
it stops existing:

```
Container removed: my-docker-session (exit 137, SIGKILL, lifetime 5.798s, oomKilled=false)
```

**171.4** Signal decoding is hoisted into a single `describeExitCode()` /
`describe_exit_code()`. It lives in `exit-reason.js` / `exit_reason.rs` rather
than the log-utils module the issue suggested, because `SIGNAL_NAMES` already
lives there and that module is dependency-free — putting it in log-utils created
an import cycle. Log-utils re-exports it, so both call sites the issue names are
satisfied. The watcher's shell `case` table is *generated from the same table*,
so the log and `--status` can never name different signals for the same code.

**171.5** `exitReason` is persisted alongside the record.

## Beyond the two sub-issues

The **attached** Docker path had the same gap: it inspected `State.OOMKilled`
alone, so its "Container kept for investigation" message could not say what
killed the container, and a removed one took its facts with it. It now reads the
same five fields in one inspect, before any `docker rm`, and reuses the same
formatters. `readDockerContainerOomKilled` / `read_docker_container_oom_killed`
are gone — the new reader returns that flag alongside the rest.

Docker's zero-time sentinel `0001-01-01T00:00:00Z` is rejected everywhere, so a
year-1 timestamp can never reach a record or a log.

## Dependencies

None added, after checking the alternatives: `dockerode` / `bollard` would
replace a tiny `sh -c` watcher that must *outlive* the CLI process, which is the
one thing a library bound to that process cannot do; `docker events` has the
same lifetime problem; and a ten-entry signal table does not justify a `signal` /
`nix` dependency.

## How to reproduce

```bash
$ --detached --docker -- sh -c 'sleep 1; exit 137'
$ --status <uuid>          # before: status executing, endTime = now, different on every call
$ --status <uuid>          # after:  status executed, exitCode 137 (SIGKILL - 128+9),
                           #         endTime fixed, endTimeSource docker-finished-at
cat <logPath>              # after:  === Container post-mortem === before the footer
```

## Tests

New, written before the fixes:

- `js/test/regression-170.js` — 10 tests
- `js/test/regression-171.js` — 22 tests (6 cover the attached path)
- `rust/tests/regression_170.rs` — 9 tests
- `rust/tests/regression_171.rs` — 12 tests, including `/bin/sh` execution of the
  generated snippets against a fake `docker` on `PATH`
- watcher-shape and attached-path unit tests in `docker-cleanup.js` /
  `docker_cleanup.rs` (the Rust generators are `pub(crate)`, so those assertions
  have to live in-file)
- `rust/tests/cleanup.rs` and `js/test/execution-store.js` updated for the new
  `staleDetectedAt` semantics

Local verification: JS `bun run check` clean, 953 pass / 0 fail across 53 files;
Rust `cargo fmt`/`cargo clippy --all-targets` clean, 862 pass / 0 fail; file-size
check and test parity (932 Rust / 902 JS = 103.3%) both pass.

## Note on file splits

Two files crossed the repository's 1000-line limit and were split along their
existing seams: `isolation.rs` → `isolation_shell.rs`, and `status_formatter.rs`
→ `status_footer.rs` (footer parsing) + `status_probe.rs` (live backend
probing). No behaviour moved with them.

Fixes #170
Fixes #171
Fixes #172

issue.body:
## Summary

Repository-mode PR for #172: one pull request implementing both sub-issues, in
**both** implementations (JavaScript and Rust), plus the attached-Docker path
the sub-issues do not mention but which had the same defect.

Neither sub-issue was already resolved — both were reproduced with failing
tests before anything was fixed.

## #170 — the detached terminal state was never persisted

A detached Docker execution's completion watcher streamed the logs, decided on
cleanup, wrote the footer — and then left the store record `executing` forever.
`--status` papered over the gap by calling the clock at query time, so every
query invented a different "finish" time for the same finished command.

**170.1 — write the terminal state back into the store.**
The watcher now re-invokes the CLI once the container is gone and persists
`status`, the real `exitCode`, `oomKilled` and a real `endTime`. Bookkeeping
runs **last**, after the log footer, so a record only becomes terminal once its
log is complete — asserted by comparing string offsets in the generated script.

Dispatch differs by necessity: JavaScript re-invokes `detached-finalize.js`
through the runtime, Rust re-invokes its own binary via `current_exe()` with a
hidden `--internal-finalize-detached-docker` flag, handled before argument
parsing so it never appears in `--help`.

**170.2 — stop calling `new Date()` at query time.**
Precedence is `State.FinishedAt` → the log footer's `Finished:` line →
observation time, and the result is *marked*: `endTimeSource` is one of
`docker-finished-at`, `log-footer`, `observed-at`, and the last also sets
`observedAt`. The footer parser returns both facts (exit code *and* timestamp)
instead of the exit code alone.

Root cause found while wiring this up: the shell footer snippet used local
`date` while the in-process footer wrote UTC, so the two writers of the same
`Finished:` line disagreed on timezone. Both now use `date -u`.

**170.3 — `cleanupStale` must not fabricate a finish time.**
A lost execution now keeps `endTime` empty and records `staleDetectedAt`. The
moment cleanup noticed is not the moment the command stopped, and conflating
them is exactly the bug this issue is about.

**170.4 — signal deaths.**
Taken as the documented option: `status` answers one question — *is this still
running?* — and README now says so explicitly. The cause of death is carried by
`exitCode` (decoded: `137 (SIGKILL - 128+9)`), `oomKilled`, `exitReason` and the
post-mortem. Adding `killed`/`terminated` statuses would have made `status` a
verdict again, which #148/#151/#162/#165 deliberately moved away from.

## #171 — "Container kept for investigation" omitted the post-mortem

**171.1** The watcher's single `docker inspect` now collects
`{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.StartedAt}} {{.State.FinishedAt}}`
plus `{{.State.Error}}` (read separately — it is free-form text that can contain
spaces, so it cannot ride along in a whitespace-split template).

**171.2** A kept container's log ends with the facts, before the footer:

```
=== Container post-mortem ===
Container:  my-docker-session
Exit Code:  137 (SIGKILL - 128+9)
OOMKilled:  false
StartedAt:  2026-09-15T22:21:40.942007645Z
FinishedAt: 2026-09-15T22:21:46.740817278Z
Lifetime:   5.798s
Error:      (none)
```

**171.3** A removed container states the same facts in one line, written before
it stops existing:

```
Container removed: my-docker-session (exit 137, SIGKILL, lifetime 5.798s, oomKilled=false)
```

**171.4** Signal decoding is hoisted into a single `describeExitCode()` /
`describe_exit_code()`. It lives in `exit-reason.js` / `exit_reason.rs` rather
than the log-utils module the issue suggested, because `SIGNAL_NAMES` already
lives there and that module is dependency-free — putting it in log-utils created
an import cycle. Log-utils re-exports it, so both call sites the issue names are
satisfied. The watcher's shell `case` table is *generated from the same table*,
so the log and `--status` can never name different signals for the same code.

**171.5** `exitReason` is persisted alongside the record.

## Beyond the two sub-issues

The **attached** Docker path had the same gap: it inspected `State.OOMKilled`
alone, so its "Container kept for investigation" message could not say what
killed the container, and a removed one took its facts with it. It now reads the
same five fields in one inspect, before any `docker rm`, and reuses the same
formatters. `readDockerContainerOomKilled` / `read_docker_container_oom_killed`
are gone — the new reader returns that flag alongside the rest.

Docker's zero-time sentinel `0001-01-01T00:00:00Z` is rejected everywhere, so a
year-1 timestamp can never reach a record or a log.

## Dependencies

None added, after checking the alternatives: `dockerode` / `bollard` would
replace a tiny `sh -c` watcher that must *outlive* the CLI process, which is the
one thing a library bound to that process cannot do; `docker events` has the
same lifetime problem; and a ten-entry signal table does not justify a `signal` /
`nix` dependency.

## How to reproduce

```bash
$ --detached --docker -- sh -c 'sleep 1; exit 137'
$ --status <uuid>          # before: status executing, endTime = now, different on every call
$ --status <uuid>          # after:  status executed, exitCode 137 (SIGKILL - 128+9),
                           #         endTime fixed, endTimeSource docker-finished-at
cat <logPath>              # after:  === Container post-mortem === before the footer
```

## Tests

New, written before the fixes:

- `js/test/regression-170.js` — 10 tests
- `js/test/regression-171.js` — 22 tests (6 cover the attached path)
- `rust/tests/regression_170.rs` — 9 tests
- `rust/tests/regression_171.rs` — 12 tests, including `/bin/sh` execution of the
  generated snippets against a fake `docker` on `PATH`
- watcher-shape and attached-path unit tests in `docker-cleanup.js` /
  `docker_cleanup.rs` (the Rust generators are `pub(crate)`, so those assertions
  have to live in-file)
- `rust/tests/cleanup.rs` and `js/test/execution-store.js` updated for the new
  `staleDetectedAt` semantics

Local verification: JS `bun run check` clean, 953 pass / 0 fail across 53 files;
Rust `cargo fmt`/`cargo clippy --all-targets` clean, 862 pass / 0 fail; file-size
check and test parity (932 Rust / 902 JS = 103.3%) both pass.

## Note on file splits

Two files crossed the repository's 1000-line limit and were split along their
existing seams: `isolation.rs` → `isolation_shell.rs`, and `status_formatter.rs`
→ `status_footer.rs` (footer parsing) + `status_probe.rs` (live backend
probing). No behaviour moved with them.

Fixes #170
Fixes #171
Fixes #172
